Explore larger models optimized for multi-step reasoning to reveal stronger or more specialized reasoning signals.
Investigate how higher-level representations in deeper layers (beyond reasoning saturation) might align with cortical hierarchies or large-scale cognitive organization.
papers.abstract: Understanding how the human brain progresses from processing simple linguistic inputs to performing high-level reasoning is a fundamental challenge in neuroscience. While modern large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to model neural responses to language, their internal representations are highly "entangled," mixing information about lexicon, syntax, meaning, and reasoning. This entanglement biases conventional brain encoding analyses toward linguistically shallow features (e.g., lexicon and syntax), making it difficult to isolate the neural substrates of cognitively deeper processes. Here, we introduce a residual disentanglement method that computationally isolates these components. By first probing an LM to identify feature-specific layers, our method iteratively regresses out lower-level representations to produce four nearly orthogonal embeddings for lexicon, syntax, meaning, and, critically, reasoning. We used these disentangled embeddings to model intracranial (ECoG) brain recordings from neurosurgical patients listening to natural speech. We show that: 1) This isolated reasoning embedding exhibits unique predictive power, accounting for variance in neural activity not explained by other linguistic features and even extending to the recruitment of visual regions beyond classical language areas. 2) The neural signature for reasoning is temporally distinct, peaking later (~350-400ms) than signals related to lexicon, syntax, and meaning, consistent with its position atop a processing hierarchy. 3) Standard, non-disentangled LLM embeddings can be misleading, as their predictive success is primarily attributable to linguistically shallow features, masking the more subtle contributions of deeper cognitive processing.

papers.title: Locating and Editing Factual Associations in GPT
papers.research_question: How are factual associations stored and recalled in autoregressive transformer language models, and can they be directly edited?
papers.core_contribution: Factual associations in GPT are stored in mid-layer feed-forward modules and can be directly edited using a rank-one update method (ROME), which achieves strong generalization and specificity.
papers.conclusion: Factual associations in autoregressive transformers are stored in mid-layer MLP modules and can be directly edited via localized weight updates, with ROME providing an effective method for such edits.
papers.key_findings:
Causal tracing reveals that mid-layer MLP modules at the last subject token are decisive for factual predictions.
The Rank-One Model Editing (ROME) method can effectively edit factual associations by updating a single MLP layer with a rank-one weight update.
ROME achieves strong generalization and specificity on counterfactual edits, outperforming previous fine-tuning and hypernetwork-based methods.
The early site (mid-layer MLP) and late site (late-layer attention) play different roles: MLP stores the association, and attention copies it to the output.
The paper introduces a new dataset, COUNTERFACT, for evaluating counterfactual model edits.
papers.limitation: Human evaluation reveals a reduction in fluency of generated text under ROME, which the automatic entropy measure does not capture.
papers.abstract: We analyze the storage and recall of factual associations in autoregressive transformer language models, finding evidence that these associations correspond to localized, directly-editable computations. We first develop a causal intervention for identifying neuron activations that are decisive in a model's factual predictions. This reveals a distinct set of steps in middle-layer feed-forward modules that mediate factual predictions while processing subject tokens. To test our hypothesis that these computations correspond to factual association recall, we modify feed-forward weights to update specific factual associations using Rank-One Model Editing (ROME). We find that ROME is effective on a standard zero-shot relation extraction (zsRE) model-editing task, comparable to existing methods. To perform a more sensitive evaluation, we also evaluate ROME on a new dataset of counterfactual assertions, on which it simultaneously maintains both specificity and generalization, whereas other methods sacrifice one or another. Our results confirm an important role for mid-layer feed-forward modules in storing factual associations and suggest that direct manipulation of computational mechanisms may be a feasible approach for model editing. The code, dataset, visualizations, and an interactive demo notebook are available at https://rome.baulab.info/

papers.title: Understanding Reasoning in Thinking Language Models via Steering Vectors
papers.research_question: Can reasoning behaviors in thinking language models be controlled using steering vectors?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that reasoning behaviors in thinking LLMs are mediated by linear directions in the activation space and can be controlled using steering vectors extracted via difference of means and attribution patching.
papers.conclusion: Steering vectors provide a practical method for controlling reasoning behaviors in thinking models, opening new possibilities for fine-grained control of model behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Thinking models exhibit distinct reasoning behaviors such as backtracking, uncertainty estimation, and example testing.
These behaviors are mediated by linear directions in the model's activation space.
Steering vectors extracted via difference of means can control these behaviors, increasing or decreasing their occurrence.
The steering approach works across different model architectures within the DeepSeek-R1-Distill family.
The method provides a practical tool for modulating reasoning capabilities in thinking models.
papers.limitation:
The automated annotation process using GPT-4o has occasionally produced false positives and false negatives in identifying reasoning patterns.
The generalization of these findings to other models that have undergone reward-based RL training instead of being fine-tuned on thinking models remains an open question.
future_direction: Developing more robust annotation methods, potentially incorporating multiple models or human validation.
Extending the research to a broader range of models to understand the universality of thinking mechanisms.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have led to the development of thinking language models that generate extensive internal reasoning chains before producing responses. While these models achieve improved performance, controlling their reasoning processes remains challenging. This work presents a steering approach for thinking LLMs by analyzing and manipulating specific reasoning behaviors in DeepSeek-R1-Distill models. Through a systematic experiment on 500 tasks across 10 diverse categories, we identify several reasoning behaviors exhibited by thinking models, including expressing uncertainty, generating examples for hypothesis validation, and backtracking in reasoning chains. We demonstrate that these behaviors are mediated by linear directions in the model's activation space and can be controlled using steering vectors. By extracting and applying these vectors, we provide a method to modulate specific aspects of the model's reasoning process, such as its tendency to backtrack or express uncertainty. Our approach offers practical tools for steering reasoning processes in thinking models in a controlled and interpretable manner. We validate our steering method using three DeepSeek-R1-Distill models, demonstrating consistent control across different model architectures.

papers.title: On Identifiability in Transformers
papers.research_question: What is the identifiability of attention weights and token embeddings in Transformers, and how does context aggregate into hidden tokens?
papers.core_contribution: Attention weights are not identifiable and thus not directly interpretable; effective attention and hidden token attribution are proposed as tools to better understand transformers.
papers.conclusion: Attention distributions are not directly interpretable due to non-identifiability; effective attention and hidden token attribution are useful tools for understanding transformers, and the relationship between token mixing and identifiability warrants further investigation.
papers.key_findings:
Attention weights are not identifiable for sequences longer than the attention head dimension, meaning there are infinitely many attention weights yielding the same output.
Effective attention, which removes the null space component, can diverge from raw attention and provide more reliable explanations.
Contextual word embeddings retain their identity (input token) to a large degree across layers, with identity information encoded in the angle.
Input tokens mix strongly in hidden embeddings, with the contribution of the original token decreasing monotonically with depth but remaining the largest individual contributor in most cases.
Context aggregated into hidden embeddings is mostly local, with long-range dependencies increasing in later layers.
papers.limitation:
Effective attention is not guaranteed to be a probability distribution and may have negative weights.
The relationship between token mixing and identifiability warrants further investigation.
future_direction: Further research to understand effective attention and its variants.
Applying the concepts to compare different transformer variants.
papers.abstract: In this paper we delve deep in the Transformer architecture by investigating two of its core components: self-attention and contextual embeddings. In particular, we study the identifiability of attention weights and token embeddings, and the aggregation of context into hidden tokens. We show that, for sequences longer than the attention head dimension, attention weights are not identifiable. We propose effective attention as a complementary tool for improving explanatory interpretations based on attention. Furthermore, we show that input tokens retain to a large degree their identity across the model. We also find evidence suggesting that identity information is mainly encoded in the angle of the embeddings and gradually decreases with depth. Finally, we demonstrate strong mixing of input information in the generation of contextual embeddings by means of a novel quantification method based on gradient attribution. Overall, we show that self-attention distributions are not directly interpretable and present tools to better understand and further investigate Transformer models.

papers.title: Knowing Before Saying: LLM Representations Encode Information About Chain-of-Thought Success Before Completion
papers.research_question: Can the success of a zero-shot Chain-of-Thought process be predicted before completion, and do LLMs encode information about reasoning success in their internal representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that LLM internal representations encode information about Chain-of-Thought success before generation, and a probing classifier can predict success, enabling potential early stopping.
papers.conclusion: The success of CoT reasoning can be predicted from LLM internal representations before generation, and these findings may inform methods to make CoT more efficient without sacrificing performance.
papers.key_findings:
A probing classifier based on LLM internal representations can predict CoT success before any token generation with 60% to 76.4% accuracy.
Internal representations outperform a BERT baseline that relies on generated tokens, indicating they encode deeper reasoning dynamics.
Providing later reasoning steps does not always improve prediction accuracy, and when it doesn't, earlier representations are more similar to later ones.
Early stopping experiments show that truncating CoT reasoning still improves performance over not using CoT, though a gap remains compared to full reasoning.
The model's intermediate representations may encode sufficient information for correct answers, but zero-shot early stopping is suboptimal.
papers.limitation:
The test set for Mistral-7B was annotated by GPT-4o mini, which may be less reliable than human annotation, and results should be interpreted with caution.
Zero-shot early stopping is a suboptimal intervention because the model does not always converge to a stable answer even when nearly the entire reasoning sequence is generated.
future_direction: Using supervised learning to train the model to generate concise reasoning chains.
Using reinforcement learning to reinforce brevity via rewards.
papers.abstract: We investigate whether the success of a zeroshot Chain-of-Thought (CoT) process can be predicted before completion.We discover that a probing classifier, based on LLM representations, performs well even before a single token is generated, suggesting that crucial information about the reasoning process is already present in the initial steps representations.In contrast, a strong BERT-based baseline, which relies solely on the generated tokens, performs worse-likely because it depends on shallow linguistic cues rather than deeper reasoning dynamics.Surprisingly, using later reasoning steps does not always improve classification.When additional context is unhelpful, earlier representations resemble later ones more, suggesting LLMs encode key information early.This implies reasoning can often stop early without loss.To test this, we conduct early stopping experiments, showing that truncating CoT reasoning still improves performance over not using CoT at all, though a gap remains compared to full reasoning.However, approaches like supervised learning or reinforcement learning designed to shorten CoT chains could leverage our classifier's guidance to identify when early stopping is effective.Our findings provide insights that may support such methods, helping to optimize CoT's efficiency while preserving its benefits.

papers.title: Large Language Models Are Cross-Lingual Knowledge-Free Reasoners
papers.research_question: What is the relationship between cross-lingual transferability and the components of reasoning tasks (knowledge retrieval vs. knowledge-free reasoning)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that knowledge-free reasoning capability transfers nearly perfectly across languages, whereas knowledge retrieval significantly hinders cross-lingual transfer, attributed to shared neural mechanisms for reasoning and language-specific knowledge storage.
papers.conclusion: The demand for knowledge retrieval significantly hinders cross-lingual transfer performance, while knowledge-free reasoning ability can be nearly fully transferred between languages, due to shared neural mechanisms for reasoning and language-specific knowledge storage.
papers.key_findings:
The knowledge retrieval component significantly hinders cross-lingual transfer in reasoning tasks; more knowledge retrieval leads to lower transfer effectiveness.
Knowledge-free reasoning capability can be nearly perfectly transferred across languages after fine-tuning in one language.
Cross-lingual computational similarity (hidden states and neuron activation) is higher for knowledge-free reasoning than for knowledge retrieval, especially in middle layers.
Target language proficiency impacts transferability; improving proficiency enhances cross-lingual transfer for knowledge-free reasoning.
The model uses similar neurons for knowledge-free reasoning across languages, while knowledge is stored separately in different languages.
papers.limitation:
Limited model selection and language coverage, primarily relying on LLaMA-2 and only ten languages.
Depth of interpretability analysis is limited; macro-level numerical analyses without precisely identifying specific neurons.
future_direction: Conduct more detailed neuron-level analyses to verify hypotheses about shared neurons for reasoning and language-specific knowledge storage.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models have demonstrated impressive reasoning capabilities across multiple languages. However, the relationship between capabilities in different languages is less explored. In this work, we decompose the process of reasoning tasks into two separated components: knowledge retrieval and knowledge-free reasoning, and analyze the relationship between cross-lingual transferability and these two components. With adapted commonsense reasoning datasets and constructed knowledge-free reasoning datasets, we show that the knowledge-free reasoning capability can be nearly perfectly transferred across various source-target language directions despite the secondary impact of resource in some specific target languages, while cross-lingual knowledge retrieval significantly hinders the transfer. Moreover, by analyzing the hidden states and feed-forward network neuron activation during the reasoning, we show that higher similarity of hidden representations and larger overlap of activated neurons could explain the better cross-lingual transferability of knowledge-free reasoning than knowledge retrieval. Thus, we hypothesize that knowledge-free reasoning shares similar neurons in different languages for reasoning, while knowledge is stored separately in different languages. Our code and data is available at: https://github.com/NJUNLP/Knowledge-Free-Reasoning.

papers.title: On the Representational Capacity of Neural Language Models with Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
papers.research_question: What is the representational capacity of neural language models (LMs) when augmented with chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning? Specifically, can CoT-augmented LMs represent the same family of distributions over strings as probabilistic Turing machines?
papers.core_contribution: This paper formalizes chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning in a probabilistic setting and shows that recurrent and transformer language models augmented with CoT reasoning can represent the same family of distributions over strings as probabilistic Turing machines.
papers.conclusion: CoT reasoning increases the computational power of neural language models by allowing them to perform additional sequential computation and keep track of execution trajectories, effectively introducing non-determinism and enabling simulation of probabilistic Turing machines.
papers.key_findings:
CoT-augmented constant-precision RNN LMs are equivalent to probabilistic finite-state automata (PFSAs), whereas without CoT they are equivalent to deterministic PFSAs.
CoT-augmented RNN LMs with linearly bounded precision and transformer LMs with logarithmically bounded precision can simulate any probabilistic Turing machine.
CoT reasoning provides a principled way to overcome the limitation of deterministic computation in fixed-precision neural models, allowing them to simulate non-deterministic automata.

papers.title: Language Models Are Greedy Reasoners: A Systematic Formal Analysis of Chain-of-Thought
papers.research_question: To what extent do large language models (LLMs) reason via chain-of-thought prompting, and do they rely on simple heuristics rather than genuine reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the PRONTO QA dataset and uses formal analysis to show that LLMs are capable of correct individual deduction steps but struggle with proof planning when multiple valid steps are available.
papers.conclusion: While the largest LLMs are generally capable of reasoning, they have difficulty with proof planning and selecting the correct proof step when multiple options are available.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs are capable of making valid individual proof steps, even in fictional contexts.
LLMs have difficulty with proof planning: when multiple valid proof steps are available, they often select the wrong step, leading to incomplete proofs.
Real-world knowledge helps reasoning: performance is significantly better with true ontologies compared to fictional or false ones.
Longer proofs (5 hops) are challenging, especially with top-down traversal of the ontology.
For larger models, the main source of error is misleading steps rather than invalid steps.
papers.limitation: The analysis is limited to modus ponens, proof lengths of at most 5, and semantically simple sentences.
future_direction: Use PRONTO QA to compare LLM reasoning with human reasoning and explore which aspects of human reasoning LLMs acquired.
Develop reasoning systems with more sophisticated proof planning/search strategies, such as neurosymbolic approaches.
Investigate whether LLMs can produce longer proofs, reason with other deduction rules, or handle more semantically complex sentences.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown remarkable reasoning capabilities given chain-of-thought prompts (examples with intermediate reasoning steps). Existing benchmarks measure reasoning ability indirectly, by evaluating accuracy on downstream tasks such as mathematical reasoning. However, it is unclear how these models obtain the answers and whether they rely on simple heuristics rather than the generated chain-of-thought. To enable systematic exploration of the reasoning ability of LLMs, we present a new synthetic question-answering dataset called PrOntoQA, where each example is generated from a synthetic world model represented in first-order logic. This allows us to parse the generated chain-of-thought into symbolic proofs for formal analysis. Our analysis on InstructGPT and GPT-3 shows that LLMs are quite capable of making correct individual deduction steps, and so are generally capable of reasoning, even in fictional contexts. However, they have difficulty with proof planning: When multiple valid deduction steps are available, they are not able to systematically explore the different options.

papers.title: How do Transformers Learn Implicit Reasoning?
papers.research_question: How do transformers learn implicit reasoning, specifically multi-hop implicit reasoning, and what are the internal mechanisms that enable this ability?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals a three-stage developmental trajectory for implicit reasoning in transformers (memorization, in-distribution generalization, cross-distribution generalization) and introduces two diagnostic tools (cross-query semantic patching, cosine-based representational lens) that link representational clustering to reasoning capability.
papers.conclusion: Implicit reasoning in transformers is driven by the clustering of intermediate representations in cosine space, and generalization patterns depend on representational alignment, offering insights into the interpretability of multi-hop reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Implicit reasoning emerges in three distinct stages: memorization, in-distribution generalization, and cross-distribution generalization.
Training with atomic triples accelerates learning but is not strictly necessary for in-distribution generalization.
Second-hop generalization requires query-level exposure to specific compositional structures; exposure to the same fact in other roles is insufficient.
Intermediate entity representations are located in middle layers (e.g., layer 5 at the r1 token) and are not necessarily decodable via logit lens, indicating a gap between explicit decodability and functional usage.
Successful reasoning correlates with cosine-space clustering of intermediate representations; generalization patterns depend on representational alignment driven by in-distribution supervision.
papers.limitation: The study uses a controlled symbolic environment, which is simpler than the rich and complex knowledge bases of real LLMs, so the findings are preliminary and may not fully explain reasoning dynamics in LLMs.
papers.abstract: Recent work suggests that large language models (LLMs) can perform multi-hop reasoning implicitly -- producing correct answers without explicitly verbalizing intermediate steps -- but the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. In this paper, we study how such implicit reasoning emerges by training transformers from scratch in a controlled symbolic environment. Our analysis reveals a three-stage developmental trajectory: early memorization, followed by in-distribution generalization, and eventually cross-distribution generalization. We find that training with atomic triples is not necessary but accelerates learning, and that second-hop generalization relies on query-level exposure to specific compositional structures. To interpret these behaviors, we introduce two diagnostic tools: cross-query semantic patching, which identifies semantically reusable intermediate representations, and a cosine-based representational lens, which reveals that successful reasoning correlates with the cosine-base clustering in hidden space. This clustering phenomenon in turn provides a coherent explanation for the behavioral dynamics observed across training, linking representational structure to reasoning capability. These findings provide new insights into the interpretability of implicit multi-hop reasoning in LLMs, helping to clarify how complex reasoning processes unfold internally and offering pathways to enhance the transparency of such models.

papers.title: Schoenfeld's Anatomy of Mathematical Reasoning by Language Models
papers.research_question: Do reasoning traces exhibit consistent structure when abstracted into functional episodes? How do reasoning dynamics differ across models? How do episode patterns correlate with correctness and efficiency?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ThinkARM, a framework for abstracting reasoning traces into functional episodes, enabling systematic analysis of reasoning structure and dynamics in LLMs.
papers.conclusion: Episode-level representations make reasoning steps explicit, enabling systematic analysis of how reasoning is structured, stabilized, and altered in modern language models.
papers.key_findings:
Episode-level analysis reveals a functional progression from abstract reasoning to concrete execution to evaluative control.
Reasoning models distribute effort across analysis, exploration, execution, and verification, while non-reasoning models are heavily execution-focused.
Exploration serves as a critical branching point: correct solutions route exploration into monitoring or re-analysis, while incorrect ones tend to continue execution or terminate.
Efficient reasoning methods selectively suppress evaluation-oriented episodes and feedback loops, diverging from base model patterns.
papers.abstract: Large language models increasingly expose reasoning traces, yet their underlying cognitive structure and steps remain difficult to identify and analyze beyond surface-level statistics. We adopt Schoenfeld's Episode Theory as an inductive, intermediate-scale lens and introduce ThinkARM (Anatomy of Reasoning in Models), a scalable framework that explicitly abstracts reasoning traces into functional reasoning steps such as Analysis, Explore, Implement, Verify, etc. When applied to mathematical problem solving by diverse models, this abstraction reveals reproducible thinking dynamics and structural differences between reasoning and non-reasoning models, which are not apparent from token-level views. We further present two diagnostic case studies showing that exploration functions as a critical branching step associated with correctness, and that efficiency-oriented methods selectively suppress evaluative feedback steps rather than uniformly shortening responses. Together, our results demonstrate that episode-level representations make reasoning steps explicit, enabling systematic analysis of how reasoning is structured, stabilized, and altered in modern language models.

papers.title: KisMATH: Do LLMs Have Knowledge of Implicit Structures in Mathematical Reasoning?
papers.research_question: How does chain-of-thought (CoT) work in LLMs for mathematical reasoning? Specifically, are reasoning nodes in CoT traces causal contributors to the final answer, and do LLMs internally realize structures similar to extracted causal graphs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Causal CoT Graphs (CCGraphs) to extract fine-grained causal dependencies from reasoning traces, and shows that reasoning nodes are causal contributors to the final answer and that LLMs internally realize structures similar to CCGraphs.
papers.conclusion: LLMs have knowledge of implicit structures in mathematical reasoning, and CCGraphs capture these structures, providing a causal view of CoT reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Reasoning nodes in CCGraphs are causal mediators for the final answer, a necessary condition for reasoning.
LLMs emphasize reasoning paths captured by CCGraphs, indicating internal realization of such structures.
Mathematical expressions play a more significant role than natural language glue in simpler problems (GSM8K), but both are important in complex problems (AIME, MATH500).
Models exhibit two behavior modes in path probability distributions: bell-shaped and exponential-shaped, related to uncertainty and exploration.
Models with higher uncertainty along reasoning paths (bell-shaped) show better exploration and improved performance with more samples.
papers.limitation:
Manual interventions were required for some graphs due to parsing errors or natural language interruptions.
Geometry problems were filtered out due to challenges in parsing.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) traces have been shown to improve performance of large language models on a plethora of reasoning tasks, yet there is no consensus on the mechanism by which this boost is achieved. To shed more light on this, we introduce Causal CoT Graphs (CCGraphs), which are directed acyclic graphs automatically extracted from reasoning traces that model fine-grained causal dependencies in language-model outputs. A collection of 1671 mathematical reasoning problems from MATH500, GSM8K, and AIME, together with their associated CCGraphs, has been compiled into our dataset -- KisMATH. Our detailed empirical analysis with 15 open-weight LLMs shows that (i) reasoning nodes in the CCGraphs are causal contributors to the final answer, which we argue is constitutive of reasoning; and (ii) LLMs emphasize the reasoning paths captured by the CCGraphs, indicating that the models internally realize structures similar to our graphs. KisMATH enables controlled, graph-aligned interventions and opens avenues for further investigation into the role of CoT in LLM reasoning.

papers.title: Deep Hidden Cognition Facilitates Reliable Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
papers.research_question: Can the model’s internal activations effectively distinguish between truthful and false branches in CoT reasoning, and can these signals be used to guide more reliable CoT decoding?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a method that leverages the model's internal truthfulness sensitivity, identified via probing attention heads, to train a confidence predictor. This predictor is then used to guide beam search during CoT generation, significantly enhancing the reliability of CoT reasoning by reducing error accumulation.
papers.conclusion: The proposed method, which leverages internal truthfulness signals to train a confidence predictor and guide CoT generation, significantly enhances the reliability of CoT reasoning across diverse tasks and models.
papers.key_findings:
The model's internal activations during CoT reasoning encode truthfulness information, which can be extracted via probing attention heads.
A confidence predictor trained on these activations outperforms baselines like sequence likelihood and verbalized confidence in calibration metrics.
Integrating the confidence predictor into a beam search framework for CoT generation improves reasoning accuracy across diverse unimodal and multimodal tasks and model scales.
The method is compatible with self-correction techniques and generalizes to specialized reasoning models like DeepSeek R1.
papers.abstract: Chain of Thought (CoT) reasoning has demonstrated remarkable deep reasoning capabilities in both large language models (LLMs) and multimodal large language models (MLLMs). However, its reliability is often undermined by the accumulation of errors in intermediate steps. This paper introduces an novel approach to calibrate the CoT reasoning accuracy by leveraging the model's intrinsic veracity encoding. We discover that specific attention head activations reliably reflect the truthfulness of reasoning steps in CoT. Based on this insight, we train a confidence predictor to evaluate the correctness of each reasoning step using these truthfulness-sensitive activations, dynamically selecting the most plausible reasoning path via beam search. Experimental results demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art baselines (e.g., Few-Shot CoT, Self-Consistency, and Self-Evaluation Guided Beam Search) across the mathematical, symbolic, and commonsense reasoning tasks, exhibiting superior accuracy and reliability in both unimodal and multimodal settings. We further validate the approach on large reasoning models, confirming its applicability to specialized reasoning models. Additionally, we explore the role of the model's self-correction ability in CoT reasoning. This work provides a novel reliability improvement path for CoT reasoning with broad application potential.

papers.title: Understanding the role of FFNs in driving multilingual behaviour in LLMs
papers.research_question: How do Feed-Forward Networks (FFNs) in large language models drive multilingual behavior, and what are the patterns of multilingual processing across layers and model sizes?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the metric 'activation flatness' and analyzes FFN sublayers (detectors and combinators) to reveal distinct patterns of multilingual processing, identifying the phenomenon of 'over-layerization' where increasing layer depth without other adjustments can degrade performance.
papers.conclusion: The analysis reveals distinct patterns in FFN sublayers for multilingual processing, with detectors becoming more peaked and language-specific in later layers, and combinators showing multilingual behavior in middle layers, while also identifying over-layerization in certain model configurations.
papers.key_findings:
FFN representations are more sparse near the input and output layers across all models.
Detector activations become more peaked (less flat) through the layers, while combinator activations show a distinct drop in flatness around layer 20 regardless of model size.
Early detector layers are multilingual and process shallow features, becoming more language-specific near the output.
Combinator layers are mostly multilingual in the middle layers, with the final layers becoming language-specific, especially in larger models.
The 2.9B parameter model exhibits 'over-layerization', where increased layer depth without corresponding adjustments leads to degraded generation quality compared to the 7.5B model.
papers.limitation:
The analysis relies only on model snapshots (activations), which does not fully capture the complexities of LLMs; probing tasks or attention matrices could provide a more comprehensive understanding.
The investigation is limited to the XGLM model family, and findings may not generalize to other LLM architectures or implementations.
The analysis is limited to a set of predefined languages and test sets, which may not fully represent linguistic diversity.
future_direction: Investigate whether flatter activation patterns are easier to adapt in QLoRA fine-tuning.
Extend the analysis to more languages and explore cross-linguistic variation in more detail.
papers.abstract: Multilingualism in Large Language Models (LLMs) is an yet under-explored area. In this paper, we conduct an in-depth analysis of the multilingual capabilities of a family of a Large Language Model, examining its architecture, activation patterns, and processing mechanisms across languages. We introduce novel metrics to probe the model's multilingual behaviour at different layers and shed light on the impact of architectural choices on multilingual processing. Our findings reveal different patterns of multilinugal processing in the sublayers of Feed-Forward Networks of the models. Furthermore, we uncover the phenomenon of "over-layerization" in certain model configurations, where increasing layer depth without corresponding adjustments to other parameters may degrade model performance. Through comparisons within and across languages, we demonstrate the interplay between model architecture, layer depth, and multilingual processing capabilities of LLMs trained on multiple languages.

papers.title: Improving Reasoning Performance in Large Language Models via Representation Engineering
papers.research_question: Can reasoning performance in LLMs be improved by applying control vectors derived from model activations to the residual stream during inference?
papers.core_contribution: Reasoning performance in LLMs can be improved by applying control vectors derived from model activations to the residual stream during inference, without any additional training.
papers.conclusion: The experiments indicate that reasoning can in part be understood to be encoded in the residual stream, similarly to how emotional valence or other features are encoded, and can be modulated via representation engineering.
papers.key_findings:
Control vectors derived from contrastive pairs or PCA can improve model performance on inductive, deductive, and mathematical reasoning tasks.
The intervention generalizes across tasks: control vectors from bAbI improve GSM8K performance and vice versa.
The intervention changes the model's internal representations, as evidenced by changes in KL divergence and entropy.
The method requires no additional training and works by adding control vectors to the residual stream during inference.
The optimal scaling factor α varies across models and tasks.
papers.limitation:
Limited scope of models (smaller than production-level state-of-the-art models).
The IOI task is relatively simple, which limits the scope of potential errors and the generalizability of findings.
The need for better contrastive pairs for reasoning to optimally derive control vectors.
future_direction: Applying the intervention to much larger models.
Applying the intervention to more general tasks.
Testing different contrastive schemes.
Exploring ways of embedding this methodology into the models.
papers.abstract: Recent advancements in large language models (LLMs) have resulted in increasingly anthropomorphic language concerning the ability of LLMs to reason. Whether reasoning in LLMs should be understood to be inherently different is, however, widely debated. We propose utilizing a representation engineering approach wherein model activations are read from the residual stream of an LLM when processing a reasoning task. The activations are used to derive a control vector that is applied to the model as an inference-time intervention, modulating the representational space of the model, to improve performance on the specified task. We publish the code for deriving control vectors and analyzing model representations. The method allows us to improve performance on reasoning benchmarks and assess how control vectors influence the final logit distribution of a model via metrics such as KL divergence and entropy. We apply control vectors to Mistral-7B-Instruct and a range of Pythia models on an inductive, a deductive and mathematical reasoning task. We show that an LLM can, to a certain degree, be controlled to improve its perceived reasoning ability by modulating activations. The intervention is dependent upon the ability to reliably extract the model's typical state when correctly solving a task. Our results suggest that reasoning performance can be modulated in the same manner as other information-processing tasks performed by LLMs and demonstrate that we are capable of improving performance on specific tasks via a simple intervention on the residual stream with no additional training.

papers.title: Arithmetic Without Algorithms: Language Models Solve Math With a Bag of Heuristics
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) solve arithmetic reasoning tasks by learning robust generalizable algorithms or by memorizing training data?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs solve arithmetic tasks by combining a sparse set of heuristic neurons, each implementing simple patterns, forming a 'bag of heuristics' rather than using a robust algorithm or memorization.
papers.conclusion: LLMs implement a bag of heuristics—a combination of many memorized rules—to perform arithmetic reasoning, rather than using robust algorithms or pure memorization.
papers.key_findings:
A sparse subset of MLP neurons in the arithmetic circuit implements simple heuristics for arithmetic.
Each heuristic neuron activates for specific input patterns and promotes corresponding answer tokens.
The combination of these heuristic neurons (a bag of heuristics) explains most of the model's accuracy on arithmetic prompts.
This mechanism emerges early in training and persists as the main source of arithmetic accuracy.
The bag of heuristics fails to generalize perfectly, leading to errors when prompts lack sufficient associated heuristics or when heuristics have imperfect recall.
papers.limitation:
Human bias in defining heuristic types, as abstractions are based on human-identifiable definitions.
Analysis focuses on LLMs that tokenize multi-digit numbers as single tokens, which may not generalize to models with single-digit tokenization.
future_direction: Developing methods to identify heuristic abstractions without human bias.
Investigating if regularization can improve the bag of heuristics mechanism.
Exploring fundamental changes to training and architectures to improve mathematical abilities.
papers.abstract: Do large language models (LLMs) solve reasoning tasks by learning robust generalizable algorithms, or do they memorize training data? To investigate this question, we use arithmetic reasoning as a representative task. Using causal analysis, we identify a subset of the model (a circuit) that explains most of the model's behavior for basic arithmetic logic and examine its functionality. By zooming in on the level of individual circuit neurons, we discover a sparse set of important neurons that implement simple heuristics. Each heuristic identifies a numerical input pattern and outputs corresponding answers. We hypothesize that the combination of these heuristic neurons is the mechanism used to produce correct arithmetic answers. To test this, we categorize each neuron into several heuristic types-such as neurons that activate when an operand falls within a certain range-and find that the unordered combination of these heuristic types is the mechanism that explains most of the model's accuracy on arithmetic prompts. Finally, we demonstrate that this mechanism appears as the main source of arithmetic accuracy early in training. Overall, our experimental results across several LLMs show that LLMs perform arithmetic using neither robust algorithms nor memorization; rather, they rely on a "bag of heuristics".

papers.title: Progress measures for grokking via mechanistic interpretability
papers.research_question: How can we find continuous progress measures that underlie seemingly discontinuous qualitative changes (like grokking) in neural networks? The paper uses mechanistic interpretability to reverse-engineer learned behaviors and define such progress measures.
papers.core_contribution: The paper uses mechanistic interpretability to define progress measures for grokking, showing that grokking arises from the gradual amplification of structured mechanisms (a Fourier multiplication algorithm) followed by removal of memorizing components, rather than being a sudden shift.
papers.conclusion: Grokking is not a sudden shift but results from gradual mechanisms, and mechanistic interpretability can reveal progress measures that track the development of emergent behavior.
papers.key_findings:
The transformers implement modular addition using a Fourier multiplication algorithm that maps inputs to a circle and uses trigonometric identities.
The model's weights and activations show periodic structure and are sparse in the Fourier domain, with key frequencies.
Two progress measures (restricted loss and excluded loss) improve continuously prior to grokking, revealing hidden progress.
Training can be split into three phases: memorization, circuit formation, and cleanup.
The sudden transition to perfect test accuracy occurs during cleanup, after the generalizing mechanism is already learned.
papers.limitation: There is significant uncertainty about the scalability of mechanistic interpretability approaches to large models.
future_direction: Apply the approach to more complex tasks and models.
Use progress measures to predict and understand emergent behavior in large language models.
Explore task-independent progress measures.
papers.abstract: Neural networks often exhibit emergent behavior, where qualitatively new capabilities arise from scaling up the amount of parameters, training data, or training steps. One approach to understanding emergence is to find continuous \textit{progress measures} that underlie the seemingly discontinuous qualitative changes. We argue that progress measures can be found via mechanistic interpretability: reverse-engineering learned behaviors into their individual components. As a case study, we investigate the recently-discovered phenomenon of ``grokking'' exhibited by small transformers trained on modular addition tasks. We fully reverse engineer the algorithm learned by these networks, which uses discrete Fourier transforms and trigonometric identities to convert addition to rotation about a circle. We confirm the algorithm by analyzing the activations and weights and by performing ablations in Fourier space. Based on this understanding, we define progress measures that allow us to study the dynamics of training and split training into three continuous phases: memorization, circuit formation, and cleanup. Our results show that grokking, rather than being a sudden shift, arises from the gradual amplification of structured mechanisms encoded in the weights, followed by the later removal of memorizing components.

papers.title: Causal Abstraction for Chain-of-Thought Reasoning in Arithmetic Word Problems
papers.research_question: How do chain-of-thought (CoT) prompts improve LLMs' accuracy on arithmetic word problems, and do LLMs actually use their CoTs to reason to their final answers?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides evidence that CoT-prompted LLMs use their generated chain-of-thought tokens to reason to final answers in arithmetic word problems, as shown through causal abstraction analysis.
papers.conclusion: LLMs achieve higher accuracy with CoT prompting, correct answers correlate with correct CoTs, and LLMs partially realize the causal models from their CoTs, suggesting they use CoTs to reason, though for some LLMs other processes may also play a role.
papers.key_findings:
CoT prompting significantly improves LLM accuracy on the GSM8K test set compared to non-CoT prompting.
Correct final answers are highly correlated with correctly formulated and executed CoTs.
LLMs realize the causal models suggested by their CoTs to a fairly large extent, indicating causal impact of CoT tokens on final answers.
For Cohere Command and PaLM Bison, higher degrees of realization are associated with better overall accuracy.
For OpenAI GPT-3.5, other internal processes may be involved, as shown by intervention-ignoring and self-correcting behavior.
papers.limitation:
Only examines a few LLMs' behavior for a small subset of examples from a single dataset.
Limited to one type of reasoning task (multi-step arithmetic) and may not generalize to other tasks.
Experiments conducted in a controlled setting with temperature 0, so findings may not extend to settings with randomness.
Only found evidence of partial realizations, and the theoretical interpretation of such partial realizations is unclear.
future_direction: Scale up to more examples with more robust human evaluation methods.
Explore cases where LLMs produce incorrect CoTs to examine if they still realize the causal models.
Replicate experiments with LLMs whose internal representations are accessible.
papers.abstract: Recent work suggests that large language models (LLMs) achieve higher accuracy on multi-step reasoning tasks when prompted to generate intermediate reasoning steps, or a chain of thought (CoT), before their final answer. However, it is unclear how exactly CoTs improve LLMs’ accuracy, and in particular, if LLMs use their CoTs to reason to their final answers. This paper tries to answer this question with respect to arithmetic word problems, by (i) evaluating the correctness of LLMs’ CoTs, and (ii) using causal abstraction to assess if the intermediate tokens produced as part of a CoT causally impact LLMs’ final answers, in line with the reasoning described by the CoT. We find that for CoT-prompted LLMs, correct answers to arithmetic problems are highly correlated with correct CoTs, and that when LLMs produce correct CoTs, they realize to a fairly large extent the causal models suggested by their CoTs. Higher degrees of realization also seem associated with better overall accuracy on the arithmetic problems. These findings suggest that some CoT-prompted LLMs may do better on multi-step arithmetic reasoning at least partly because they use their CoTs to reason to their final answers. However, for some LLMs, other internal processes may also be involved.

papers.title: Internal Chain-of-Thought: Empirical Evidence for Layer-wise Subtask Scheduling in LLMs
papers.research_question: Do large language models perform multi-step reasoning internally, breaking down composite tasks and processing components sequentially across network layers?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models exhibit an internal chain-of-thought, where distinct subtasks are learned at different network depths and executed sequentially across layers.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit an internal chain-of-thought, sequentially decomposing and executing composite tasks layer-by-layer, which enhances model transparency and enables instruction-level activation steering.
papers.key_findings:
Subtasks are learned at different network depths, as shown by layer-from context-masking revealing an X-shape pattern.
Subtasks are executed sequentially across layers, with intermediate answers peaking at middle layers and final answers overtaking later, as shown by LogitLens decoding.
Cross-task patching demonstrates that composite prompts encode transferable subtask vectors, with an average strength of 0.66.
The same sequential learning dynamics are observed in the real-world TRACE benchmark for complex instruction following.
The internal chain-of-thought enhances LLM transparency and opens avenues for fine-grained activation steering.
papers.limitation:
The study focuses on two-step composite tasks; more complex multi-step tasks may exhibit different dynamics.
The analysis is limited to models up to 8B parameters; larger models may have different internal structures.
LogitLens provides only correlational evidence; more causal analysis is needed.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to more complex multi-step tasks.
Study larger models beyond 8B parameters.
Conduct more causal analysis to complement the correlational evidence from LogitLens.
papers.abstract: We show that large language models (LLMs) exhibit an $\textit{internal chain-of-thought}$: they sequentially decompose and execute composite tasks layer-by-layer. Two claims ground our study: (i) distinct subtasks are learned at different network depths, and (ii) these subtasks are executed sequentially across layers. On a benchmark of 15 two-step composite tasks, we employ layer-from context-masking and propose a novel cross-task patching method, confirming (i). To examine claim (ii), we apply LogitLens to decode hidden states, revealing a consistent layerwise execution pattern. We further replicate our analysis on the real-world $\text{TRACE}$ benchmark, observing the same stepwise dynamics. Together, our results enhance LLMs transparency by showing their capacity to internally plan and execute subtasks (or instructions), opening avenues for fine-grained, instruction-level activation steering.

papers.title: Making Reasoning Matter: Measuring and Improving Faithfulness of Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
papers.research_question: To what degree are the final answers of large language models faithful to their stated chain-of-thought reasoning steps?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces FRODO, a framework to improve the faithfulness of chain-of-thought reasoning in small language models, and uses causal mediation analysis to measure faithfulness.
papers.conclusion: The paper performs a causal mediation analysis showing variation in faithfulness across LLMs and introduces FRODO, which improves faithfulness of chain-of-thought reasoning in small LMs.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs do not reliably use their intermediate reasoning steps when generating an answer.
Instruction-tuned models have a stronger causal effect of reasoning steps on the final answer than RLHF-trained models.
FRODO outperforms strong baselines on four reasoning tasks, improving accuracy by 2-3% over standard fine-tuning.
FRODO improves robustness, showing a 4.5% improvement in controlled indirect effect, and generalizes better to out-of-distribution test sets.
FRODO's rationales are more faithful to its final answer predictions than standard supervised fine-tuning.
papers.limitation:
The causal analysis metric does not evaluate the model's real internal reasoning process.
The method requires additional counterfactual data generated by LLMs, which can be expensive.
Training time increases as training Direct Preference Optimization is a two-step process.
Experiments were run with only 3 random seeds due to complexity.
FRODO is dependent on rationales generated by LLMs, so extra care is needed in production environments.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been shown to perform better when asked to reason step-by-step before answering a question. However, it is unclear to what degree the model's final answer is faithful to the stated reasoning steps. In this paper, we perform a causal mediation analysis on twelve LLMs to examine how intermediate reasoning steps generated by the LLM influence the final outcome and find that LLMs do not reliably use their intermediate reasoning steps when generating an answer. To address this issue, we introduce FRODO, a framework to tailor small-sized LMs to generate correct reasoning steps and robustly reason over these steps. FRODO consists of an inference module that learns to generate correct reasoning steps using an implicit causal reward function and a reasoning module that learns to faithfully reason over these intermediate inferences using a counterfactual and causal preference objective. Our experiments show that FRODO significantly outperforms four competitive baselines. Furthermore, FRODO improves the robustness and generalization ability of the reasoning LM, yielding higher performance on out-of-distribution test sets. Finally, we find that FRODO's rationales are more faithful to its final answer predictions than standard supervised fine-tuning.

papers.title: CryptoX : Compositional Reasoning Evaluation of Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we quantify the compositional reasoning capacity of large language models, and what are the inner mechanisms involved in compositional reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CryptoX, a framework to evaluate compositional reasoning in LLMs by transforming existing benchmarks with cryptographic encoding, and finds that most LLMs have weak compositional reasoning abilities, with a significant gap between open-source and closed-source models.
papers.conclusion: Highlights the value of independently studying compositional reasoning and emphasizes the need to enhance the compositional reasoning abilities of LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Most existing LLMs have weak compositional reasoning abilities, and the proposed CryptoBench can measure the gap between different models.
Compositional reasoning ability is influenced by various factors such as model size, architecture, and instruction fine-tuning.
Instruct fine-tuning enhances the compositional reasoning ability of models compared to base models.
Multi-turn decomposition of tasks is simpler for models than single-turn compositional reasoning, indicating limitations in compositional reasoning.
Layers of LLMs exhibit a clear hierarchical pattern of executing different subtasks in different layers and then aggregating for compositional reasoning.
papers.abstract: The compositional reasoning capacity has long been regarded as critical to the generalization and intelligence emergence of large language models LLMs. However, despite numerous reasoning-related benchmarks, the compositional reasoning capacity of LLMs is rarely studied or quantified in the existing benchmarks. In this paper, we introduce CryptoX, an evaluation framework that, for the first time, combines existing benchmarks and cryptographic, to quantify the compositional reasoning capacity of LLMs. Building upon CryptoX, we construct CryptoBench, which integrates these principles into several benchmarks for systematic evaluation. We conduct detailed experiments on widely used open-source and closed-source LLMs using CryptoBench, revealing a huge gap between open-source and closed-source LLMs. We further conduct thorough mechanical interpretability experiments to reveal the inner mechanism of LLMs' compositional reasoning, involving subproblem decomposition, subproblem inference, and summarizing subproblem conclusions. Through analysis based on CryptoBench, we highlight the value of independently studying compositional reasoning and emphasize the need to enhance the compositional reasoning capabilities of LLMs.

papers.title: Demystifying Reasoning Dynamics with Mutual Information: Thinking Tokens are Information Peaks in LLM Reasoning
papers.research_question: What are the critical reasoning steps or intermediate states that significantly affect the final results in the reasoning process of large reasoning models (LRMs)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers that during the reasoning process of large reasoning models (LRMs), certain steps exhibit sudden increases in mutual information (MI) with the correct answer, and these MI peaks correspond to 'thinking tokens' (e.g., 'Hmm', 'Wait') that are critical for reasoning performance. Based on this, the paper proposes two training-free methods to improve reasoning.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that thinking tokens, which correspond to MI peaks, are crucial for LRM reasoning and that leveraging these tokens can improve reasoning performance without additional training.
papers.key_findings:
During LRM reasoning, certain steps show sudden and significant increases in mutual information (MI) with the golden answer, termed MI peaks.
The tokens at MI peaks are often reflective or transitional words (e.g., 'Hmm', 'Wait', 'So') and are critical for reasoning performance; suppressing them significantly harms performance.
Theoretically, higher cumulative MI between representations and the golden answer leads to tighter bounds on prediction error.
Non-reasoning LLMs do not exhibit clear MI peaks, suggesting the phenomenon is a result of reasoning-intensive training.
Two proposed methods, Representation Recycling (RR) and Thinking Token based Test-time Scaling (TTTS), which leverage thinking tokens, can improve reasoning performance on math benchmarks.
papers.abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities in complex problem-solving, yet their internal reasoning mechanisms remain poorly understood. In this paper, we investigate the reasoning trajectories of LRMs from an information-theoretic perspective. By tracking how mutual information (MI) between intermediate representations and the correct answer evolves during LRM reasoning, we observe an interesting MI peaks phenomenon: the MI at specific generative steps exhibits a sudden and significant increase during LRM's reasoning process. We theoretically analyze such phenomenon and show that as MI increases, the probability of model's prediction error decreases. Furthermore, these MI peaks often correspond to tokens expressing reflection or transition, such as ``Hmm'', ``Wait'' and ``Therefore,'' which we term as the thinking tokens. We then demonstrate that these thinking tokens are crucial for LRM's reasoning performance, while other tokens has minimal impacts. Building on these analyses, we propose two simple yet effective methods to improve LRM's reasoning performance, by delicately leveraging these thinking tokens. Overall, our work provides novel insights into the reasoning mechanisms of LRMs and offers practical ways to improve their reasoning capabilities. The code is available at https://github.com/ChnQ/MI-Peaks.

papers.title: Scaling Reasoning Hop Exposes Weaknesses: Demystifying and Improving Hop Generalization in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: The paper investigates where errors occur in reasoning hop generalization (RQ1) and why these errors arise (RQ2), focusing on the internal mechanisms of LLMs.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes Test-time Correction of Reasoning (TCR), a lightweight intervention method that dynamically identifies and deactivates erroneous processing heads to improve reasoning hop generalization, based on mechanistic insights into internal competition mechanisms.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that TCR effectively improves reasoning hop generalization by dynamically deactivating erroneous processing heads, demonstrating the potential of test-time interventions based on mechanistic insights.
papers.key_findings:
Errors in reasoning hop generalization are dominated by token-level erroneous predictions of a few specific error types, enabling focused diagnosis.
These token-level errors stem from an internal competition mechanism: correct trajectories coexist with erroneous ones but are actively suppressed by erroneous processing heads; knocking out such heads can restore correct predictions.
The proposed TCR method, which automatically and dynamically deactivates erroneous processing heads, consistently improves reasoning hop generalization across tasks and models.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning has become the standard paradigm for enabling Large Language Models (LLMs) to solve complex problems. However, recent studies reveal a sharp performance drop in reasoning hop generalization scenarios, where the required number of reasoning steps exceeds training distributions while the underlying algorithm remains unchanged. The internal mechanisms driving this failure remain poorly understood. In this work, we conduct a systematic study on tasks from multiple domains, and find that errors concentrate at token positions of a few critical error types, rather than being uniformly distributed. Closer inspection reveals that these token-level erroneous predictions stem from internal competition mechanisms: certain attention heads, termed erroneous processing heads (ep heads), tip the balance by amplifying incorrect reasoning trajectories while suppressing correct ones. Notably, removing individual ep heads during inference can often restore the correct predictions. Motivated by these insights, we propose test-time correction of reasoning, a lightweight intervention method that dynamically identifies and deactivates ep heads in the reasoning process. Extensive experiments across different tasks and LLMs show that it consistently improves reasoning hop generalization, highlighting both its effectiveness and potential.

papers.title: Finite State Automata Inside Transformers with Chain-of-Thought: A Mechanistic Study on State Tracking
papers.research_question: Does Chain-of-Thought (CoT) help transformers recover a world model in the form of finite state automata (FSAs), or do they merely learn shortcuts?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer+CoT learns implicit finite state automata (FSAs) for state tracking, as evidenced by mechanistic analysis showing that late-layer MLP neurons implement state transitions and exhibit compression and distinction properties.
papers.conclusion: Transformer+CoT achieves near-perfect next-token prediction while internalizing an FSA-like structured state representation, bridging the gap between theoretical expressiveness and practical learnability.
papers.key_findings:
Transformer+CoT efficiently learns state tracking for sequences of arbitrary length across multiple groups (Z60, A4 × Z5, A5), outperforming other architectures like RNNs and transformer variants.
The circuit for state tracking relies heavily on late-layer MLP neurons, with MLP11 playing a key role.
Neurons in late-layer MLPs can be classified into states based on transition rules with high accuracy, indicating an N-to-1 mapping between neurons and states.
The model exhibits near-perfect compression and distinction metrics, providing evidence that it recovers an implicit FSA structure.
The learned FSAs are robust to skipping intermediate steps and noise in scratchpads, but struggle with generalization to significantly longer sequences.
papers.limitation: The model struggles with generalization to significantly longer sequences.
future_direction: Modifications to model architecture, loss functions, or optimization algorithms to improve length generalization.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) significantly enhances the performance of large language models (LLMs) across a wide range of tasks, and prior research shows that CoT can theoretically increase expressiveness. However, there is limited mechanistic understanding of the algorithms that Transformer+CoT can learn. Our key contributions are: (1) We evaluate the state tracking capabilities of Transformer+CoT and its variants, confirming the effectiveness of CoT. (2) Next, we identify the circuit (a subset of model components, responsible for tracking the world state), indicating that late-layer MLP neurons play a key role. We propose two metrics, compression and distinction, and show that the neuron sets for each state achieve nearly 100% accuracy, providing evidence of an implicit finite state automaton (FSA) embedded within the model. (3) Additionally, we explore three challenging settings: skipping intermediate steps, introducing data noises, and testing length generalization. Our results demonstrate that Transformer+CoT learns robust algorithms (FSAs), highlighting its resilience in challenging scenarios. Our code is available at https://github.com/IvanChangPKU/FSA.

papers.title: Deciphering the Factors Influencing the Efficacy of Chain-of-Thought: Probability, Memorization, and Noisy Reasoning
papers.research_question: What factors influence the efficacy of Chain-of-Thought prompting in Large Language Models? Specifically, does CoT performance reflect abstract reasoning or shallow heuristics?
papers.core_contribution: CoT prompting performance in LLMs is influenced by three factors: the probability of the correct output, memorization of frequent patterns from pre-training, and noisy reasoning where error rate increases with task difficulty.
papers.conclusion: CoT prompting performance reflects both memorization and a probabilistic version of genuine reasoning, supporting a middle-ground viewpoint in the debate about LLM reasoning capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
CoT performance is affected by the probability of the correct output, with higher probability outputs leading to higher accuracy.
Memorization plays a role, as evidenced by a spike in accuracy for shift level 13 (rot-13), which is common in internet text and training data.
Noisy reasoning is observed: accuracy decreases as the number of implicit reasoning steps (shift level) increases, indicating a noisy reasoning process.
Unfaithfulness between intermediate reasoning steps and the final answer occurs, especially for low-probability outputs, where the model may 'self-correct' to a higher-probability word.
CoT can be effective even when the demonstration in the prompt is invalid, suggesting the format of reasoning steps is more important than their correctness.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting has been shown to enhance the multi-step reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs). However, debates persist about whether LLMs exhibit abstract generalization or rely on shallow heuristics when given CoT prompts. To understand the factors influencing CoT reasoning we provide a detailed case study of the symbolic reasoning task of decoding shift ciphers, where letters are shifted forward some number of steps in the alphabet. We analyze the pattern of results produced by three LLMs -- GPT-4, Claude 3, and Llama 3.1 -- performing this task using CoT prompting. By focusing on a single relatively simple task, we are able to identify three factors that systematically affect CoT performance: the probability of the task's expected output (probability), what the model has implicitly learned during pre-training (memorization), and the number of intermediate operations involved in reasoning (noisy reasoning). We show that these factors can drastically influence task accuracy across all three LLMs; e.g., when tested with GPT-4, varying the output's probability of occurrence shifts accuracy from 26% to 70%. Overall, we conclude that CoT prompting performance reflects both memorization and a probabilistic version of genuine reasoning. Code and data at this https://github.com/aksh555/deciphering_cot

papers.title: Interpretability in the Wild: a Circuit for Indirect Object Identification in GPT-2 small
papers.research_question: How does GPT-2 small perform the indirect object identification (IOI) task, and what internal circuit is responsible for this behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies and validates a circuit of 26 attention heads in GPT-2 small that performs indirect object identification, using a combination of interpretability techniques and quantitative criteria for faithfulness, completeness, and minimality.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that mechanistic understanding of large ML models is feasible, providing a step towards scaling interpretability to larger models and more complex tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Discovered a circuit of 26 attention heads grouped into 7 classes (e.g., Name Mover Heads, S-Inhibition Heads) that implement the IOI task.
Identified redundant behavior such as Backup Name Mover Heads that activate when regular Name Mover Heads are ablated.
Found that Negative Name Mover Heads write in the opposite direction, potentially to hedge predictions.
Formulated and evaluated quantitative criteria (faithfulness, completeness, minimality) to validate circuit explanations.
The circuit shows significant but incomplete understanding, with gaps in completeness and minimality.
papers.limitation:
Not fully understanding some components, such as the attention patterns of S-Inhibition Heads and the role of MLPs and layer norms.
The circuit is not completely complete or minimal, as shown by quantitative criteria.
The analysis is limited to GPT-2 small, which is much smaller than state-of-the-art models.
future_direction: Scale the approach to larger models like GPT-2 medium.
Investigate the behavior of the circuit on adversarial examples.
Understand the compensation effect in Backup Name Mover Heads.
papers.abstract: Research in mechanistic interpretability seeks to explain behaviors of machine learning models in terms of their internal components. However, most previous work either focuses on simple behaviors in small models, or describes complicated behaviors in larger models with broad strokes. In this work, we bridge this gap by presenting an explanation for how GPT-2 small performs a natural language task called indirect object identification (IOI). Our explanation encompasses 26 attention heads grouped into 7 main classes, which we discovered using a combination of interpretability approaches relying on causal interventions. To our knowledge, this investigation is the largest end-to-end attempt at reverse-engineering a natural behavior "in the wild" in a language model. We evaluate the reliability of our explanation using three quantitative criteria--faithfulness, completeness and minimality. Though these criteria support our explanation, they also point to remaining gaps in our understanding. Our work provides evidence that a mechanistic understanding of large ML models is feasible, opening opportunities to scale our understanding to both larger models and more complex tasks.

papers.title: The Reasoning-Memorization Interplay in Language Models Is Mediated by a Single Direction
papers.research_question: What are the precise conditions under which LLMs switch between reasoning and memorization during text generation, and can we identify linear features that mediate this interplay?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies linear reasoning features (LiReFs) in the residual stream of LLMs that mediate the switch between reasoning and memorization, and shows that intervening on these features can improve reasoning performance and generalizability.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that linear reasoning features in the residual stream mediate the reasoning-memorization interplay in LLMs, and that targeted intervention on these features can enhance reasoning performance and generalizability, offering insights for more robust and interpretable AI systems.
papers.key_findings:
Linear Reasoning Features (LiReFs) can be extracted from the residual stream by contrasting reasoning-intensive and memory-intensive questions.
LiReFs separate questions by their required capability (reasoning vs. memory) across domains and languages.
The activation along LiReFs correlates with the reasoning score assigned by GPT-4o, indicating a spectrum from memory to reasoning.
Inference-time intervention on LiReFs (adding or ablating) can improve model performance on both memory and reasoning tasks.
LiReF intervention enhances genuine reasoning generalizability, as shown on GSM-Symbolic, and reduces reasoning errors.
papers.limitation: The study's definition of memorization as poor generalizability may not capture other forms of memorization (e.g., counterfactual memorization).
future_direction: Investigate whether perturbational and counterfactual memorization are mechanistically equivalent and mediated by LiReFs.
Extend the LiReF analysis to more models and tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel on a variety of reasoning benchmarks, but previous studies suggest they sometimes struggle to generalize to unseen questions, potentially due to over-reliance on memorized training examples. However, the precise conditions under which LLMs switch between reasoning and memorization during text generation remain unclear. In this work, we provide a mechanistic understanding of LLMs' reasoning-memorization dynamics by identifying a set of linear features in the model's residual stream that govern the balance between genuine reasoning and memory recall. These features not only distinguish reasoning tasks from memory-intensive ones but can also be manipulated to causally influence model performance on reasoning tasks. Additionally, we show that intervening in these reasoning features helps the model more accurately activate the most relevant problem-solving capabilities during answer generation. Our findings offer new insights into the underlying mechanisms of reasoning and memory in LLMs and pave the way for the development of more robust and interpretable generative AI systems.

papers.title: The Same But Different: Structural Similarities and Differences in Multilingual Language Modeling
papers.research_question: When two languages employ the same morphosyntactic processes, do LLMs handle them using shared internal circuitry? When two languages require different morphosyntactic processes, do LLMs handle them using different internal circuitry?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that LLMs use shared internal circuitry for similar syntactic processes across languages, even in independently trained monolingual models, and employ language-specific components (e.g., feed-forward networks) for language-specific morphological processes.
papers.conclusion: The paper finds that cross-lingual structural similarity is represented within LLMs using shared circuits that invoke the same algorithm independent of language, and that language-specific processing is localized to play a causal role only in languages that require it.
papers.key_findings:
Multilingual models use a single circuit to handle the same syntactic process independently of the language in which it occurs.
Monolingual models trained independently on English and Chinese each adopt nearly the same circuit for the IOI task, suggesting consistency in how LLMs learn to handle this aspect of language modeling.
For tasks requiring language-specific morphological processes (e.g., past tense marking in English), multilingual models invoke a largely overlapping circuit but employ language-specific components as needed, such as feed-forward networks in English only for morphological marking.
The circuits identified for the IOI task align with prior work, indicating that the same mechanism is shared between English and Chinese within a multilingual model.
Heads specifically responsible for past tense disambiguation are activated in English but not in Chinese, and they suppress present-tense verbs in English.
papers.limitation: Results are limited to specific tasks and datasets, requiring future work for replication and generalization.
future_direction: Replicate and generalize findings to more tasks and datasets.
Explore cross-disciplinary collaborations to gain fresh perspectives on linguistic universality using LLMs.
Investigate whether circuit overlap can be exploited for improving cross-lingual transfer and safety.
papers.abstract: We employ new tools from mechanistic interpretability in order to ask whether the internal structure of large language models (LLMs) shows correspondence to the linguistic structures which underlie the languages on which they are trained. In particular, we ask (1) when two languages employ the same morphosyntactic processes, do LLMs handle them using shared internal circuitry? and (2) when two languages require different morphosyntactic processes, do LLMs handle them using different internal circuitry? Using English and Chinese multilingual and monolingual models, we analyze the internal circuitry involved in two tasks. We find evidence that models employ the same circuit to handle the same syntactic process independently of the language in which it occurs, and that this is the case even for monolingual models trained completely independently.
