By establishing a shared vocabulary between cognitive science and LLM research, our framework enables systematic diagnosis of reasoning failures and principled development of models that reason through robust cognitive mechanisms rather than spurious shortcuts, while providing tools to test theories of human cognition at scale.

papers.title: Understanding and Steering the Cognitive Behaviors of Reasoning Models at Test-Time
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often rely on long chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning to solve complex tasks. While effective, these trajectories are frequently inefficient, leading to high latency from excessive token generation, or unstable reasoning that alternates between underthinking (shallow, inconsistent steps) and overthinking (repetitive, verbose reasoning). In this work, we study the structure of reasoning trajectories and uncover specialized attention heads that correlate with distinct cognitive behaviors such as verification and backtracking. By lightly intervening on these heads at inference time, we can steer the model away from inefficient modes. Building on this insight, we propose CREST, a training-free method for Cognitive REasoning Steering at Test-time. CREST has two components: (1) an offline calibration step that identifies cognitive heads and derives head-specific steering vectors, and (2) an inference-time procedure that rotates hidden representations to suppress components along those vectors. CREST adaptively suppresses unproductive reasoning behaviors, yielding both higher accuracy and lower computational cost. Across diverse reasoning benchmarks and models, CREST improves accuracy by up to 17.5% while reducing token usage by 37.6%, offering a simple and effective pathway to faster, more reliable LLM reasoning.

papers.title: Large Language Models are In-Context Semantic Reasoners rather than Symbolic Reasoners
papers.research_question: Are LLMs good in-context reasoners without semantics?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that semantics are vital for LLMs' in-context reasoning; they perform well when semantics align with commonsense but struggle with symbolic or counter-commonsense reasoning, relying on superficial semantic connections rather than formal symbolic reasoning.
papers.conclusion: LLMs rely heavily on learned semantics for in-context reasoning, creating strong token connections that compose a superficial logical chain, rather than performing formal symbolic reasoning like humans.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs perform significantly better on reasoning tasks when semantics are consistent with commonsense compared to when semantics are decoupled (symbolic setting).
LLMs struggle to solve symbolic or counter-commonsense reasoning tasks by leveraging in-context new knowledge.
Semantic knowledge is easier for LLMs to memorize than symbolic knowledge, but updating semantic knowledge has a higher forgetting ratio due to stronger correlations.
LLMs' reasoning performance is inferior to logic-based symbolic methods across all tested reasoning tasks (deduction, induction, abduction).
The length of the in-context information impacts reasoning performance, with shorter contexts leading to better results.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to specific datasets (Symbolic Tree, ProofWriter) and models (ChatGPT, GPT-4, LLaMA-7B).
Long-context reasoning is challenging for LLMs, as they struggle to select relevant information from excessively long prompts.
future_direction: Combining LLMs with non-parametric knowledge bases (e.g., graph databases) for more efficient and accurate knowledge updating and reasoning.
Further research on neural-symbolic AI systems to leverage the strengths of both neural and symbolic approaches.
Investigating the internal mechanisms of LLMs to better understand how they utilize semantics for reasoning.
papers.abstract: The emergent few-shot reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) have excited the natural language and machine learning community over recent years. Despite of numerous successful applications, the underlying mechanism of such in-context capabilities still remains unclear. In this work, we hypothesize that the learned \textit{semantics} of language tokens do the most heavy lifting during the reasoning process. Different from human's symbolic reasoning process, the semantic representations of LLMs could create strong connections among tokens, thus composing a superficial logical chain. To test our hypothesis, we decouple semantics from the language reasoning process and evaluate three kinds of reasoning abilities, i.e., deduction, induction and abduction. Our findings reveal that semantics play a vital role in LLMs' in-context reasoning -- LLMs perform significantly better when semantics are consistent with commonsense but struggle to solve symbolic or counter-commonsense reasoning tasks by leveraging in-context new knowledge. The surprising observations question whether modern LLMs have mastered the inductive, deductive and abductive reasoning abilities as in human intelligence, and motivate research on unveiling the magic existing within the black-box LLMs. On the whole, our analysis provides a novel perspective on the role of semantics in developing and evaluating language models' reasoning abilities. Code is available at {\url{https://github.com/XiaojuanTang/ICSR}}.

papers.title: Benchmarking and Understanding Compositional Relational Reasoning of LLMs
papers.research_question: What is the capability of existing transformer large language models (LLMs) in solving compositional relational reasoning (CRR) tasks, and what are the underlying mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the Generalized Associative Recall (GAR) benchmark for evaluating compositional relational reasoning in LLMs, revealing their deficiency, and discovers core circuits and True/False attention heads that are fundamental for CRR.
papers.conclusion: The GAR benchmark is challenging for mainstream LLMs and reveals a fundamental deficiency in compositional relational reasoning. Mechanistic interpretability analysis discovers reusable core circuits and identifies True/False attention heads that play fundamental roles in CRR across models and tasks.
papers.key_findings:
GAR is challenging for existing LLMs, with performance dropping significantly for harder tasks and the compositionality gap increasing with model scale.
Attribution patching reveals core circuits reused by Vicuna-33B across different GAR tasks, including a truthfulness sub-circuit and an in-context learning sub-circuit.
Intervention experiments show that correct functioning of identified vital attention heads (e.g., predicting, pre-predicting, higher-order local, induction, and relating heads) significantly impacts task performance.
Two classes of higher-order relating heads (True and False heads) are identified whose activations represent the abstract notion of true and false in GAR tasks.
The activation patterns of the True/False heads generalize to other datasets (SNLI and GoT), indicating they encode information for truthfulness classification beyond GAR.
papers.limitation: The circuit discovery is done manually without using automatic circuit discovery methods, which is left for future work.
future_direction: Automatic circuit discovery methods for larger models and more complex circuits.
papers.abstract: Compositional relational reasoning (CRR) is a hallmark of human intelligence, but we lack a clear understanding of whether and how existing transformer large language models (LLMs) can solve CRR tasks. To enable systematic exploration of the CRR capability of LLMs, we first propose a new synthetic benchmark called Generalized Associative Recall (GAR) by integrating and generalizing the essence of several tasks in mechanistic interpretability (MI) study in a unified framework. Evaluation shows that GAR is challenging enough for existing LLMs, revealing their fundamental deficiency in CRR. Meanwhile, it is easy enough for systematic MI study. Then, to understand how LLMs solve GAR tasks, we use attribution patching to discover the core circuits reused by Vicuna-33B across different tasks, and a set of vital attention heads. Intervention experiments show that the correct functioning of these heads significantly impacts task performance. Especially, we identify two classes of heads whose activations represent the abstract notion of true and false in GAR tasks respectively. They play fundamental roles in CRR across various models and tasks.

papers.title: Can Transformer be Too Compositional? Analysing Idiom Processing in Neural Machine Translation
papers.research_question: How does the Transformer-based neural machine translation model process idioms, and is the non-compositionality of idioms reflected in its mechanics?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer tends to translate idioms too compositionally, and when it produces non-literal translations, the encoder groups idiom parts more strongly as a single unit, with reduced interaction with context and reduced cross-attention on source tokens.
papers.conclusion: Transformer's tendency to process idioms compositionally contributes to literal translations, and techniques that encourage compositionality in NMT may be detrimental for non-compositional phenomena like idioms.
papers.key_findings:
Figurative idioms receive more attention within the PIE in encoder self-attention compared to literal idioms.
Figurative idioms have reduced attention between the PIE and its context.
In cross-attention, figurative idioms lead to reduced attention on source-side PIE tokens and increased attention on the </s> token.
Hidden representations of figurative idioms change more across layers than those of literal idioms.
Intervening with INLP to remove linearly encoded features of figurativeness can change paraphrased translations to word-for-word, indicating a causal link.
papers.limitation:
Heuristic annotation method for translations has imperfect accuracy (75-89% for key categories).
Analysis is limited to seven European languages.
future_direction: Architectural changes to improve grouping of idioms as single units, e.g., training specific attention heads or penalizing overly compositional translations.
Evaluate the effect of compositionality-favouring techniques on non-compositional phenomena like idioms.
papers.abstract: Unlike literal expressions, idioms' meanings do not directly follow from their parts, posing a challenge for neural machine translation (NMT). NMT models are often unable to translate idioms accurately and over-generate compositional, literal translations. In this work, we investigate whether the non-compositionality of idioms is reflected in the mechanics of the dominant NMT model, Transformer, by analysing the hidden states and attention patterns for models with English as source language and one of seven European languages as target language.When Transformer emits a non-literal translation - i.e. identifies the expression as idiomatic - the encoder processes idioms more strongly as single lexical units compared to literal expressions. This manifests in idioms' parts being grouped through attention and in reduced interaction between idioms and their context.In the decoder's cross-attention, figurative inputs result in reduced attention on source-side tokens. These results suggest that Transformer's tendency to process idioms as compositional expressions contributes to literal translations of idioms.

papers.title: How does Alignment Enhance LLMs' Multilingual Capabilities? A Language Neurons Perspective
papers.research_question: How does multilingual alignment enhance LLMs' multilingual capabilities from the perspective of language neurons?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a ternary classification of language neurons (specific, related, general) with an identification algorithm, and uses it to analyze how multilingual alignment enhances LLMs' capabilities by promoting shared neurons.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes a ternary neuron classification and shows that multilingual alignment enhances LLMs' multilingual capabilities by promoting shared language-related neurons, providing valuable insights into the mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Language-related neurons shared by multiple languages are crucial for multilingual performance, not just language-specific neurons.
Multilingual alignment increases the reliance on shared language-related neurons rather than language-specific neurons.
LLMs' internal multilingual inference process can be divided into four functional stages based on neuron distributions.
Alignment enhances the activation of appropriate neuron types across different stages of inference.
Spontaneous multilingual alignment is facilitated by increased sharing of language-related neurons across languages.
papers.limitation:
Limited experiments on only two models and two datasets due to resource constraints.
No finer-grained analysis of neurons within the same layer.
future_direction: Perform more comprehensive analysis on different models and datasets.
Conduct finer-grained analysis of neurons within layers.
papers.abstract: Multilingual Alignment is an effective and representative paradigm to enhance LLMs' multilingual capabilities, which transfers the capabilities from the high-resource languages to the low-resource languages. Meanwhile, some research on language-specific neurons provides a new perspective to analyze and understand LLMs' mechanisms. However, we find that there are many neurons that are shared by multiple but not all languages and cannot be correctly classified. In this work, we propose a ternary classification methodology that categorizes neurons into three types, including language-specific neurons, language-related neurons, and general neurons. And we propose a corresponding identification algorithm to distinguish these different types of neurons. Furthermore, based on the distributional characteristics of different types of neurons, we divide the LLMs' internal process for multilingual inference into four parts: (1) multilingual understanding, (2) shared semantic space reasoning, (3) multilingual output space transformation, and (4) vocabulary space outputting. Additionally, we systematically analyze the models before and after alignment with a focus on different types of neurons. We also analyze the phenomenon of ''Spontaneous Multilingual Alignment''. Overall, our work conducts a comprehensive investigation based on different types of neurons, providing empirical results and valuable insights to better understand multilingual alignment and multilingual capabilities of LLMs.

papers.title: Towards a Mechanistic Understanding of Large Reasoning Models: A Survey of Training, Inference, and Failures
papers.research_question: What are the internal mechanisms that drive the reasoning behaviors and failures of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs)?
papers.core_contribution: This survey synthesizes recent research on the mechanistic understanding of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs), organizing insights into training dynamics, reasoning mechanisms, and unintended behaviors to bridge the gap between performance and transparency.
papers.conclusion: The survey highlights the need for applied interpretability, improved methodologies, and a unified theoretical framework to advance the mechanistic understanding of LRMs.
papers.key_findings:
SFT expands exploratory paths while RL compresses them, leading to entropy reduction and performance gains.
RL training follows a two-stage process where basic skills are acquired first, followed by the emergence of reasoning abilities.
LRMs exhibit unique reasoning structures, including cyclical processes and topological properties, driven by key behavioral primitives.
Hallucinations in LRMs are influenced by RL, which reduces abstention and can increase incorrect answers.
Chain-of-thought reasoning in LRMs is often unfaithful, with a disconnect between internal states and verbalized traces.
papers.limitation:
The rapid development of LRM research means that new findings may not be captured in this survey.
The survey focuses primarily on language models, excluding multimodal capabilities.
The discussion is limited to traditional LLM architectures, excluding newer approaches like diffusion-based LLMs.
future_direction: Applied interpretability for training-time and inference-time improvements
Development of scalable and generalizable mechanistic interpretability frameworks
Establishment of a unified theoretical framework for reasoning in LRMs
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has catalyzed the emergence of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) that have pushed reasoning capabilities to new heights. While their performance has garnered significant excitement, exploring the internal mechanisms driving these behaviors has become an equally critical research frontier. This paper provides a comprehensive survey of the mechanistic understanding of LRMs, organizing recent findings into three core dimensions: 1) training dynamics, 2) reasoning mechanisms, and 3) unintended behaviors. By synthesizing these insights, we aim to bridge the gap between black-box performance and mechanistic transparency. Finally, we discuss under-explored challenges to outline a roadmap for future mechanistic studies, including the need for applied interpretability, improved methodologies, and a unified theoretical framework.

papers.title: On the Bias of Next-Token Predictors Toward Systematically Inefficient Reasoning: A Shortest-Path Case Study
papers.research_question: How does the efficiency and structure of reasoning traces (e.g., optimal dynamic programming vs. inefficient backtracking) affect the generalization and next-token prediction confidence of transformers trained on shortest-path tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that transformers trained on inefficient, systematic reasoning traces (with backtracking) generalize better than those trained on optimal dynamic programming traces, due to higher next-token prediction confidence.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that chain-of-thought is crucial for generalization, that structured but inefficient reasoning traces are more effective than globally optimal ones, and that next-token confidence predicts learnability.
papers.key_findings:
Training with intermediate reasoning traces (chain-of-thought) substantially improves generalization compared to direct question-answer training.
Models trained on inefficient depth-first search traces outperform those trained on optimal dynamic programming traces, even when trace lengths are equalized.
The benefit of inefficient traces is not due to length alone; injecting arbitrary redundancy without systematic structure can hurt performance.
Generalization correlates with next-token confidence: traces that are more predictable (systematic and locally incremental) yield higher confidence and better learning.
Models exhibit a bias towards generating longer traces, which can be regularized by sampling at non-zero temperature.
papers.limitation: The synthetic algorithmic task and custom token language may limit transferability to natural-language or multimodal settings.
future_direction: Curriculum learning or reinforcement learning to steer models toward more compact reasoning.
Mechanistic interpretability analysis to uncover circuits for reasoning.
Extending the efficiency-effectiveness trade-off study to larger models and natural-language tasks.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in natural language processing highlight two key factors for improving reasoning in large language models (LLMs): (i) allocating more test-time compute tends to help on harder problems but often introduces redundancy in the reasoning trace, and (ii) compute is most effective when reasoning is systematic and incremental, forming structured chains of thought (CoTs) akin to human problem-solving. To study these factors in isolation, we introduce a controlled setting based on shortest-path tasks in layered graphs. We train decoder-only transformers on question-trace-answer triples using a custom tokenizer, comparing models trained on optimal bottom-up dynamic programming traces with those trained on longer, valid traces involving backtracking. Surprisingly, with the same training-token budget, models trained on inefficient traces generalize better to unseen graphs. This benefit is not due to length alone-injecting arbitrary redundancy into reasoning traces fails to help and can even hurt performance. Instead, we find that generalization correlates with the model's confidence in next-token prediction, suggesting that long, coherent, and locally incremental traces make the training signal easier to optimize.

papers.title: Compositional Processing Emerges in Neural Networks Solving Math Problems
papers.research_question: Do deep neural networks evaluate arithmetic expressions using the principle of compositionality by encoding and combining partial results?
papers.core_contribution: Neural networks trained on math problems can encode partial results of sub-expressions in their internal representations, demonstrating emergent compositional processing.
papers.conclusion: Neural networks can exhibit compositional processing when trained on math problems, though imperfectly, suggesting a blend of compositional and holistic strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Models encode digit quantities in their representations, with vectors organized by numerical value.
Operators encode intermediate arithmetic results, with vector distances correlating with value differences.
These encodings are found in attention vectors, indicating compositional processing.
Compositionality is imperfect, as shown by non-zero correlations across sequences.
Both standard and TP-Transformers exhibit similar patterns of compositional encoding.
papers.limitation:
The observed compositionality is imperfect, with non-zero correlations indicating incomplete separation of sub-expressions.
Models show poor generalization on extrapolation problems with different surface features.
future_direction: Clarify whether scaling leads to human-level compositionality or if explicit design is needed.
papers.abstract: A longstanding question in cognitive science concerns the learning mechanisms underlying compositionality in human cognition. Humans can infer the structured relationships (e.g., grammatical rules) implicit in their sensory observations (e.g., auditory speech), and use this knowledge to guide the composition of simpler meanings into complex wholes. Recent progress in artificial neural networks has shown that when large models are trained on enough linguistic data, grammatical structure emerges in their representations. We extend this work to the domain of mathematical reasoning, where it is possible to formulate precise hypotheses about how meanings (e.g., the quantities corresponding to numerals) should be composed according to structured rules (e.g., order of operations). Our work shows that neural networks are not only able to infer something about the structured relationships implicit in their training data, but can also deploy this knowledge to guide the composition of individual meanings into composite wholes.

papers.title: Linear Representations of Sentiment in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How is sentiment represented within Large Language Models (LLMs)? Specifically, is it represented linearly and what are the mechanisms involved?
papers.core_contribution: This paper reveals that sentiment is represented linearly in LLMs via a single direction in activation space, demonstrates its causal relevance through interventions, and discovers a 'summarization motif' where sentiment is aggregated at intermediate tokens like commas.
papers.conclusion: The work shows that sentiment is linearly represented and causally relevant in LLMs, identifies a summarization motif, and contributes to understanding internal feature representation, suggesting directions for future interpretability research.
papers.key_findings:
Sentiment is represented linearly in LLMs: a single direction in activation space captures sentiment across tasks and models.
This sentiment direction is causally relevant for sentiment tasks, as shown by activation patching and ablation experiments.
The sentiment direction generalizes across models and out-of-distribution datasets.
The model uses a circuit involving specific attention heads and neurons to process sentiment.
The summarization motif: sentiment information is aggregated at intermediate tokens without inherent valence (e.g., commas, periods), acting as information bottlenecks.
papers.limitation:
Analysis is primarily on decoder-only models, and may not generalize to other architectures.
Toy datasets are simple and may not capture full natural language complexity.
Causal interventions may not fully capture model dynamics on more complex tasks.
future_direction: Extend methods to other features beyond sentiment, such as toxicity or deception.
Investigate the summarization motif in other tasks and models.
Develop more robust methods for finding linear directions in larger models.
papers.abstract: Sentiment is a pervasive feature in natural language text, yet it is an open question how sentiment is represented within Large Language Models (LLMs). In this study, we reveal that across a range of models, sentiment is represented linearly: a single direction in activation space mostly captures the feature across a range of tasks with one extreme for positive and the other for negative. Through causal interventions, we isolate this direction and show it is causally relevant in both toy tasks and real world datasets such as Stanford Sentiment Treebank. Through this case study we model a thorough investigation of what a single direction means on a broad data distribution. We further uncover the mechanisms that involve this direction, highlighting the roles of a small subset of attention heads and neurons. Finally, we discover a phenomenon which we term the summarization motif: sentiment is not solely represented on emotionally charged words, but is additionally summarized at intermediate positions without inherent sentiment, such as punctuation and names. We show that in Stanford Sentiment Treebank zero-shot classification, 76% of above-chance classification accuracy is lost when ablating the sentiment direction, nearly half of which (36%) is due to ablating the summarized sentiment direction exclusively at comma positions.

papers.title: Dissociation of Faithful and Unfaithful Reasoning in LLMs
papers.research_question: How do LLMs recover from errors in Chain of Thought, and what factors affect faithful versus unfaithful recovery?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides evidence that LLMs have two distinct modes of reasoning (faithful and unfaithful) when recovering from errors in chain-of-thought, and these modes respond differently to factors like error magnitude and context.
papers.conclusion: LLMs have two distinct reasoning modes: one faithful and interpretable, and one unfaithful where the generated text does not accurately represent the internal reasoning. This challenges the reliability of chain-of-thought for model auditing.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs recover more frequently from larger errors than smaller ones.
Prior expectations of errors (via context noise or prompting) increase error recovery rates.
More evidence for the correct value in the context increases error recovery rates.
Faithful and unfaithful recoveries respond differently to interventions, indicating distinct mechanisms.
Different models (GPT-4, Claude-3 Opus, Llama-3) show varying patterns in faithful vs. unfaithful recovery.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to mathematical reasoning problems and does not investigate non-mathematical reasoning errors; additionally, the introduced errors may differ from naturally occurring errors.
future_direction: Understanding the mechanisms underlying faithful and unfaithful reasoning modes
Identifying factors that influence which reasoning mode is activated
Developing techniques to encourage faithful reasoning
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often improve their performance in downstream tasks when they generate Chain of Thought reasoning text before producing an answer. We investigate how LLMs recover from errors in Chain of Thought. Through analysis of error recovery behaviors, we find evidence for unfaithfulness in Chain of Thought, which occurs when models arrive at the correct answer despite invalid reasoning text. We identify factors that shift LLM recovery behavior: LLMs recover more frequently from obvious errors and in contexts that provide more evidence for the correct answer. Critically, these factors have divergent effects on faithful and unfaithful recoveries. Our results indicate that there are distinct mechanisms driving faithful and unfaithful error recoveries. Selective targeting of these mechanisms may be able to drive down the rate of unfaithful reasoning and improve model interpretability.

papers.title: Transformers learn in-context by gradient descent
papers.research_question: How does in-context learning in Transformers work? The paper hypothesizes that Transformers implement gradient descent in their forward pass to learn from in-context data.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that Transformers trained on auto-regressive objectives implement gradient descent in their forward pass, providing a mechanistic understanding of in-context learning for regression tasks.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that in-context learning in Transformers can be understood as gradient descent in the forward pass, at least for regression tasks, providing a mechanistic understanding.
papers.key_findings:
A single linear self-attention layer can be constructed to perform one step of gradient descent on a linear regression loss.
When trained on linear regression tasks, linear self-attention-only Transformers converge to weights that match the gradient descent construction.
Multiple layers of self-attention can implement multiple steps of gradient descent and even surpass plain gradient descent by learning a curvature correction (GD++).
Transformers with MLPs can solve nonlinear regression tasks by learning linear models on deep representations.
The paper connects the induction head mechanism to in-context learning by gradient descent.
papers.limitation:
The findings on linear self-attention-only Transformers only explain a limited part of a complex process, and it may be one of many possible methods giving rise to in-context learning.
The analysis is limited to regression tasks and simple Transformer architectures.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to language modeling and other domains.
Investigating the role of softmax and LayerNorm in in-context learning.
Exploring the connection to hypernetworks and weight generation.
papers.abstract: At present, the mechanisms of in-context learning in Transformers are not well understood and remain mostly an intuition. In this paper, we suggest that training Transformers on auto-regressive objectives is closely related to gradient-based meta-learning formulations. We start by providing a simple weight construction that shows the equivalence of data transformations induced by 1) a single linear self-attention layer and by 2) gradient-descent (GD) on a regression loss. Motivated by that construction, we show empirically that when training self-attention-only Transformers on simple regression tasks either the models learned by GD and Transformers show great similarity or, remarkably, the weights found by optimization match the construction. Thus we show how trained Transformers become mesa-optimizers i.e. learn models by gradient descent in their forward pass. This allows us, at least in the domain of regression problems, to mechanistically understand the inner workings of in-context learning in optimized Transformers. Building on this insight, we furthermore identify how Transformers surpass the performance of plain gradient descent by learning an iterative curvature correction and learn linear models on deep data representations to solve non-linear regression tasks. Finally, we discuss intriguing parallels to a mechanism identified to be crucial for in-context learning termed induction-head (Olsson et al., 2022) and show how it could be understood as a specific case of in-context learning by gradient descent learning within Transformers. Code to reproduce the experiments can be found at https://github.com/google-research/self-organising-systems/tree/master/transformers_learn_icl_by_gd .

papers.title: ThinkEdit: Interpretable Weight Editing to Mitigate Overly Short Thinking in Reasoning Models
papers.abstract: Recent studies have shown that Large Language Models (LLMs) augmented with chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning demonstrate impressive problem-solving abilities. However, in this work, we identify a recurring issue where these models occasionally generate overly short reasoning, leading to degraded performance on even simple mathematical problems. Specifically, we investigate how reasoning length is embedded in the hidden representations of reasoning models and its impact on accuracy. Our analysis reveals that reasoning length is governed by a linear direction in the representation space, allowing us to induce overly short reasoning by steering the model along this direction. Building on this insight, we introduce ThinkEdit, a simple yet effective weight-editing approach to mitigate the issue of overly short reasoning. We first identify a small subset of attention heads (approximately 4%) that predominantly drive short reasoning behavior. We then edit the output projection weights of these heads to remove the short reasoning direction. With changes to only 0.2% of the model's parameters, ThinkEdit effectively reduces overly short reasoning and yields notable accuracy gains for short reasoning outputs (+6.39%), along with an overall improvement across multiple math benchmarks (+3.34%). Our findings provide new mechanistic insights into how reasoning length is controlled within LLMs and highlight the potential of fine-grained model interventions to improve reasoning quality. Our code is available at: https://github.com/Trustworthy-ML-Lab/ThinkEdit

papers.title: Visual Thoughts: A Unified Perspective of Understanding Multimodal Chain-of-Thought
papers.research_question: Is there a unified explanation for why different multimodal chain-of-thought paradigms enhance large vision-language models in distinct ways?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals that multimodal chain-of-thought reasoning improves large vision-language models by incorporating visual thoughts, which act as an intermediate cache for visual information, enabling more efficient and effective reasoning.
papers.conclusion: Visual thoughts provide a unified perspective for understanding how multimodal chain-of-thought reasoning enhances large vision-language models, acting as visual caches that improve information flow and reasoning performance.
papers.key_findings:
Removing visual thoughts from the reasoning process impairs model performance more than reasoning directly from the query alone.
Different expressions of visual thoughts (natural language, structured language, edited image, generative image) vary in effectiveness depending on task clarity and conciseness.
Visual thoughts serve as primary intermediaries, connecting input images to deeper transformer layers and facilitating advanced visual information processing.
Image-form visual thoughts consistently outperform text-form visual thoughts, especially in complex scenarios requiring detailed visual information.
Visual thoughts are more effective than simple image captions for conveying visual information in complex scenes, improving reasoning accuracy.
future_direction: Exploring the integration of multiple visual thoughts to enhance visual information transmission in multimodal chain-of-thought reasoning.
papers.abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) have achieved significant success in multimodal tasks, with multimodal chain-of-thought (MCoT) further enhancing performance and interpretability. Recent MCoT methods fall into two categories: (i) Textual-MCoT (T-MCoT), which takes multimodal input and produces textual output; and (ii) Interleaved-MCoT (I-MCoT), which generates interleaved image-text outputs. Despite advances in both approaches, the mechanisms driving these improvements are not fully understood. To fill this gap, we first reveal that MCoT boosts LVLMs by incorporating visual thoughts, which convey image information to the reasoning process regardless of the MCoT format, depending only on clarity and conciseness of expression. Furthermore, to explore visual thoughts systematically, we define four distinct forms of visual thought expressions and analyze them comprehensively. Our findings demonstrate that these forms differ in clarity and conciseness, yielding varying levels of MCoT improvement. Additionally, we explore the internal nature of visual thoughts, finding that visual thoughts serve as intermediaries between the input image and reasoning to deeper transformer layers, enabling more advanced visual information transmission. We hope that the visual thoughts can inspire further breakthroughs for future MCoT research.

papers.title: What Does BERT Look at? An Analysis of BERT’s Attention
papers.research_question: What specific linguistic features does BERT learn from unlabeled data, as revealed by its attention mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that BERT's attention heads capture syntactic and coreference information, and proposes methods for analyzing attention mechanisms to reveal this linguistic knowledge.
papers.conclusion: Attention maps contain substantial linguistic knowledge and complement other model analysis techniques, and should be part of the toolkit for understanding what neural networks learn about language.
papers.key_findings:
BERT's attention heads exhibit common patterns such as attending to delimiter tokens, specific positional offsets, or broadly attending over the whole sentence.
Certain attention heads specialize to specific syntactic relations (e.g., direct objects, determiners) with high accuracy.
One attention head performs well at coreference resolution.
An attention-based probing classifier achieves 77 UAS on dependency parsing, showing BERT's attention captures substantial syntactic information.
Attention heads in the same layer tend to behave similarly.
papers.abstract: Large pre-trained neural networks such as BERT have had great recent success in NLP, motivating a growing body of research investigating what aspects of language they are able to learn from unlabeled data. Most recent analysis has focused on model outputs (e.g., language model surprisal) or internal vector representations (e.g., probing classifiers). Complementary to these works, we propose methods for analyzing the attention mechanisms of pre-trained models and apply them to BERT. BERT's attention heads exhibit patterns such as attending to delimiter tokens, specific positional offsets, or broadly attending over the whole sentence, with heads in the same layer often exhibiting similar behaviors. We further show that certain attention heads correspond well to linguistic notions of syntax and coreference. For example, we find heads that attend to the direct objects of verbs, determiners of nouns, objects of prepositions, and coreferent mentions with remarkably high accuracy. Lastly, we propose an attention-based probing classifier and use it to further demonstrate that substantial syntactic information is captured in BERT's attention.

papers.title: Towards a Mechanistic Interpretation of Multi-Step Reasoning Capabilities of Language Models
papers.research_question: Do language models perform multi-step reasoning tasks by using a reasoning mechanism or by memorizing answers from pretraining?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces MechanisticProbe, a probing method that recovers reasoning trees from attention patterns, providing evidence that LMs perform multi-step reasoning mechanistically.
papers.conclusion: The paper shows that reasoning trees can often be detected from LM attention patterns, supporting the claim that LMs may reason mechanistically.
papers.key_findings:
MechanisticProbe can recover reasoning trees from attention patterns of GPT-2 and LLaMA for most examples.
LMs identify useful statements in bottom layers and perform reasoning steps in higher layers.
Pruning attention heads that contribute to reasoning tree detection degrades performance, indicating a causal role.
Higher probing scores correlate with higher model accuracy and robustness to noise.
Finetuned models show clearer reasoning patterns in attention than few-shot models.
papers.limitation:
The study considered fairly simple reasoning tasks.
The analysis averages over attention heads, but heads may have different functions, especially in shallow models.
The analysis is limited to single-token prediction tasks and does not cover chain-of-thought reasoning.
future_direction: Explore more challenging reasoning tasks.
Analyze reasoning in chain-of-thought prompting settings.
papers.abstract: Yifan Hou, Jiaoda Li, Yu Fei, Alessandro Stolfo, Wangchunshu Zhou, Guangtao Zeng, Antoine Bosselut, Mrinmaya Sachan. Proceedings of the 2023 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing. 2023.

papers.title: Uncovering Latent Chain of Thought Vectors in Language Models
papers.research_question: Can steering vectors derived from LM activations induce Chain-of-Thought reasoning without natural language prompting?
papers.core_contribution: Steering vectors derived from contrastive activations can induce Chain-of-Thought reasoning in frozen language models, matching or exceeding the performance of traditional CoT prompting.
papers.conclusion: Steering vector injection can effectively induce Chain-of-Thought reasoning in language models without prompting, suggesting reasoning capabilities are encoded in activation and weight space. The method matches or exceeds CoT prompting performance, with injection timing influencing results.
papers.key_findings:
Steering vector injection induces CoT reasoning without natural language prompts.
The method achieves competitive or superior performance compared to CoT prompting on GSM8k, MMLU, ARC AI2, and AGI Eval benchmarks.
The approach generalizes to unseen data, as shown on the SAT Math section of AGI Eval.
Different injection strategies (single vs. continuous) yield varying performance across benchmarks.
Steered models produce more structured, step-by-step reasoning outputs while retaining natural language fluency.
papers.limitation: Performance varies with injection strategy and may not be optimized.
future_direction: Explore different methods for injecting steering vectors to optimize performance and reliability
Investigate generalization capabilities of steering vectors across different models
Scale up the approach to larger models
papers.abstract: In this work, we examine how targeted perturbations in the activation space of Language Models (LMs) can encode complex reasoning patterns. We inject steering vectors, derived from LM activations, into LMs during inference time and study whether these vectors can induce Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning in LMs without the need for natural language prompting. We demonstrate this approach on Llama3 8B Instruct and Mistral 7B v0.2 Instruct and show that activation-space interventions achieve competitive, if not superior, performance compared to traditional CoT prompting across multiple reasoning benchmarks, including GSM8k, MMLU, AGI Eval, and ARC AI2. These findings suggest that neural network activations can encode reasoning patterns, offering a new application of activation space manipulation as a tool for tuning model behavior.

papers.title: Think-to-Talk or Talk-to-Think? When LLMs Come Up with an Answer in Multi-Hop Arithmetic Reasoning
papers.research_question: When during chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning do LLMs determine their final answer, and how causally dependent is the answer on the CoT explanation?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs compute answers iteratively during CoT generation, and the CoT explanations are faithful reflections of their internal computation, not post-hoc justifications.
papers.conclusion: LLMs compute answers iteratively during CoT, making CoT explanations faithful to the internal reasoning process.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs do not determine the final answer before CoT begins; instead, they compute sub-answers during CoT generation.
Linear probes show that answers become linearly separable in hidden states only after corresponding reasoning steps in CoT.
Causal interventions show that the final answer depends causally on the CoT part, especially the latter steps, showing recency bias.
The model's internal reasoning follows a recency bias: each step causally depends on the previous step.
For distractors (unnecessary variables), the model does not encode them in a linearly separable form, indicating efficient internal mechanisms.
papers.limitation:
The study uses synthetic arithmetic tasks, which may not generalize to natural language reasoning.
The cause of incorrect answers in some instances remains unclear.
future_direction: Investigate more complex and natural language reasoning tasks.
Detailed analysis of error cases and internal representations of digits.
papers.abstract: This study investigates the incremental, internal problem-solving process of language models (LMs) with arithmetic multi-hop reasoning as a case study. We specifically investigate when LMs internally resolve sub/whole problems through first reading the problem statements, generating reasoning chains, and achieving the final answer to mechanistically interpret LMs' multi-hop problem-solving process. Our experiments reveal a systematic incremental reasoning strategy underlying LMs. They have not derived an answer at the moment they first read the problem; instead, they obtain (sub)answers while generating the reasoning chain. Therefore, the generated reasoning chains can be regarded as faithful reflections of the model's internal computation.

papers.title: Are Transformers Able to Reason by Connecting Separated Knowledge in Training Data?
papers.research_question: When and how can transformers perform compositional reasoning by connecting fragmented knowledge, and what internal mechanisms enable this ability?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers can perform compositional reasoning on the FTCT task via few-shot chain-of-thought prompting, enabled by induction heads and attention assignment, with emergence depending on model complexity and training-testing similarity.
papers.conclusion: Transformers can reason by connecting separated knowledge when provided with few-shot chain-of-thought prompts, and this ability is facilitated by induction heads and attention assignment mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Few-shot chain-of-thought prompting enables transformers to perform compositional reasoning by revealing correct vertices order.
Compositional reasoning emerges when the relative knowledge ratio (training child chain length to testing chain length) exceeds 0.3.
Multi-layer attention mechanisms (at least 2 layers and 2 heads) are necessary for compositional reasoning.
Transformers learn an underlying program during training, implemented via induction heads for in-context learning and attention assignment for parent retrieving.
The ability to reason compositionally is robust to noise in testing data but limited when intermediate steps are incomplete.
papers.limitation: Transformers trained on FTCT exhibit limited proficiency in reasoning with incomplete intermediate steps.
papers.abstract: Humans exhibit remarkable compositional reasoning by integrating knowledge from various sources. For example, if someone learns ( B = f(A) ) from one source and ( C = g(B) ) from another, they can deduce ( C=g(B)=g(f(A)) ) even without encountering ( ABC ) together, showcasing the generalization ability of human intelligence. In this paper, we introduce a synthetic learning task, "FTCT" (Fragmented at Training, Chained at Testing), to validate the potential of Transformers in replicating this skill and interpret its inner mechanism. In the training phase, data consist of separated knowledge fragments from an overall causal graph. During testing, Transformers must infer complete causal graph traces by integrating these fragments. Our findings demonstrate that few-shot Chain-of-Thought prompting enables Transformers to perform compositional reasoning on FTCT by revealing correct combinations of fragments, even if such combinations were absent in the training data. Furthermore, the emergence of compositional reasoning ability is strongly correlated with the model complexity and training-testing data similarity. We propose, both theoretically and empirically, that Transformers learn an underlying generalizable program from training, enabling effective compositional reasoning during testing.

papers.title: Parrot Mind: Towards Explaining the Complex Task Reasoning of Pretrained Large Language Models with Template-Content Structure
papers.research_question: How can pretrained large language models learn to solve complex reasoning tasks with limited training data?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the template-content structure (T-C structure) as an intrinsic constraint in language that reduces the learning space from exponential to linear, explaining how LLMs can generalize on complex reasoning tasks with limited data.
papers.conclusion: The template-content structure provides a plausible explanation for how LLMs acquire complex reasoning abilities through language modeling, and empirical evidence supports its existence in current models.
papers.key_findings:
The T-C structure exists in current LLMs, as evidenced by lower variance in template token outputs compared to content tokens.
The T-C structure reduces the hypothesis space from exponential to linear, enabling within-task generalization.
Hierarchical T-C structure further reduces the space to logarithmic, enabling task composition across sub-tasks.
Larger models exhibit clearer T-C structure, with higher AUC in classifying template vs. content tokens.
The T-C structure explains how LLMs can perform reasoning through language modeling (parroting) by learning and reusing templates.
papers.limitation:
The T-C structure may not hold for all tasks, such as purely natural language tasks like translation or chatting.
The assumption of token-wise alignment is a simplification; semantic alignment is more realistic but introduces challenges.
The framework assumes deterministic generation, while practical models output probability distributions and use sampling.
future_direction: Extending the framework to handle sampling and probability distributions.
Investigating the disentanglement of semantic and position information in Transformers.
Applying the T-C structure to more complex tasks and real-world scenarios.
papers.abstract: The pre-trained large language models (LLMs) have shown their extraordinary capacity to solve reasoning tasks, even on tasks that require a complex process involving multiple sub-steps. However, given the vast possible generation space of all the tasks, how the pretrained model learns the reasoning ability remains an open question. We firstly propose that an intrinsic structural constraint on the generated sequence of language-based reasoning -- we called it template-content structure (T-C structure) -- is the key to explain why LLMs can solve a large number of complex reasoning problems with limited training data by showing this structure can reduce the possible space from exponential level to linear level. Furthermore, by generalizing this structure to the hierarchical case, we demonstrate that models can achieve task composition, further reducing the space needed to learn from linear to logarithmic, thereby effectively learning on complex reasoning involving multiple steps. We provide both examples and formal theory of our T-C structure. We also experimentally validate the existence of the T-C structure in some current LLMs and its effectiveness for reasoning.

papers.title: A Systematic Analysis of Morphological Content in BERT Models for Multiple Languages
papers.research_question: To what extent do BERT-style models encode morphological feature information in their hidden representations and attention distributions for multiple languages?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that BERT-style models encode morphological information by partitioning their embedding space into convex regions correlated with feature values, that contextualized embeddings help disambiguate ambiguous forms but not completely, and that specific attention head/layer combinations focus on subject-verb agreement.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that pre-trained BERT-style models are sensitive to morphological information, with strong performance on feature-value classification and certain attention heads learning to focus attention in a manner consistent with morphological agreement.
papers.key_findings:
BERT-style models partition their embedding space into convex sub-regions highly correlated with morphological feature value.
Contextualized embeddings allow models to distinguish ambiguous morphological forms in many, but not all cases.
Specific attention head/layer combinations hone in on subject-verb agreement.
Supervision significantly aids in extracting morphological information, as unsupervised clustering performs near random baselines.
Morphological information is best represented in the middle layers for languages with complex morphology (German and Russian), while for simpler languages it is present throughout all layers.
papers.limitation:
Models have difficulty disambiguating syncretic (ambiguous) forms, especially in languages with complex inflectional morphology.
The classification tasks require supervision; unsupervised methods (k-means) perform near random baselines.
future_direction: Identifying morphological information in BERT-style models in an unsupervised fashion.
Improving models' ability to disambiguate syncretic forms for languages with complex inflectional morphology.
Further exploration of how morphological information is shared between words via self-attention.
papers.abstract: This work describes experiments which probe the hidden representations of several BERT-style models for morphological content. The goal is to examine the extent to which discrete linguistic structure, in the form of morphological features and feature values, presents itself in the vector representations and attention distributions of pre-trained language models for five European languages. The experiments contained herein show that (i) Transformer architectures largely partition their embedding space into convex sub-regions highly correlated with morphological feature value, (ii) the contextualized nature of transformer embeddings allows models to distinguish ambiguous morphological forms in many, but not all cases, and (iii) very specific attention head/layer combinations appear to hone in on subject-verb agreement.

papers.title: Birth of a Transformer: A Memory Viewpoint
papers.research_question: How do transformers balance global knowledge and in-context learning during training, specifically in the development of induction head mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a synthetic bigram dataset and an associative memory viewpoint to study learning dynamics in two-layer transformers, showing that induction heads emerge through top-down gradient-based learning.
papers.conclusion: The associative memory viewpoint provides valuable insights into transformer learning dynamics, offering a foundation for better interpretability and improvements in large language models.
papers.key_findings:
Global bigram associations are learned rapidly, while in-context induction mechanisms develop more slowly.
Transformer weight matrices can be viewed as associative memories that store input-output embedding pairs.
The induction head mechanism forms in a top-down manner, with output matrices learning before key-query matrices.
Theoretical gradient analysis shows how associative memories are recovered from noisy inputs during training.
Data distribution properties, such as trigger frequency and output uniformity, affect the learning speed and accuracy of associative memories.
papers.limitation:
The simplified transformer architecture lacks components like non-linear MLPs, multiple heads, and layer normalization, which are present in standard transformers.
The synthetic dataset may not fully capture the complexity of real-world language data.
future_direction: Extending the associative memory viewpoint to non-linear components and multi-head architectures.
Applying insights to optimization algorithms, data selection, and model editing for LLMs.
Studying how such mechanisms scale to larger models and more complex tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models based on transformers have achieved great empirical successes. However, as they are deployed more widely, there is a growing need to better understand their internal mechanisms in order to make them more reliable. These models appear to store vast amounts of knowledge from their training data, and to adapt quickly to new information provided in their context or prompt. We study how transformers balance these two types of knowledge by considering a synthetic setup where tokens are generated from either global or context-specific bigram distributions. By a careful empirical analysis of the training process on a simplified two-layer transformer, we illustrate the fast learning of global bigrams and the slower development of an "induction head" mechanism for the in-context bigrams. We highlight the role of weight matrices as associative memories, provide theoretical insights on how gradients enable their learning during training, and study the role of data-distributional properties.

papers.title: Label Words are Anchors: An Information Flow Perspective for Understanding In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: How does in-context learning (ICL) work in large language models, specifically what is the role of label words in the information flow?
papers.core_contribution: Label words serve as anchors in in-context learning: they aggregate information from demonstrations in shallow layers and provide reference for predictions in deep layers.
papers.conclusion: Label words function as anchors in ICL, aggregating and distributing task-relevant information; this understanding enables improvements in accuracy, efficiency, and interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Label words aggregate information from demonstration examples in shallow transformer layers.
The model extracts information from label words in deep layers to form the final prediction.
Anchor re-weighting, which adjusts the significance of label words, improves ICL accuracy by an average of 16.7%.
Compressing demonstrations to anchor hidden states (Hiddenanchor) speeds up inference by up to 1.8× with minimal performance loss.
ICL errors can be diagnosed by analyzing distances between anchor key vectors, which correlate with category confusion.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to classification tasks and does not explore generative tasks.
Due to hardware constraints, models are limited to up to 6 billion parameters, leaving larger-scale models unexplored.
The hypothesis is only examined in conventional ICL paradigms, not in others like chain-of-thought prompting.
future_direction: Replicating the study with larger-scale models.
Exploring other ICL paradigms such as chain-of-thought prompting.
papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) emerges as a promising capability of large language models (LLMs) by providing them with demonstration examples to perform diverse tasks. However, the underlying mechanism of how LLMs learn from the provided context remains under-explored. In this paper, we investigate the working mechanism of ICL through an information flow lens. Our findings reveal that label words in the demonstration examples function as anchors: (1) semantic information aggregates into label word representations during the shallow computation layers' processing; (2) the consolidated information in label words serves as a reference for LLMs' final predictions. Based on these insights, we introduce an anchor re-weighting method to improve ICL performance, a demonstration compression technique to expedite inference, and an analysis framework for diagnosing ICL errors in GPT2-XL. The promising applications of our findings again validate the uncovered ICL working mechanism and pave the way for future studies.

papers.title: Accurate Word Alignment Induction from Neural Machine Translation
papers.research_question: Do attention weights in Transformer models capture accurate word alignments, and how can word alignments be better induced from neural machine translation models?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that Transformer attention weights can capture accurate word alignments if the correct decoding step and layer are chosen, and introduces two novel methods (SHIFT-ATT and SHIFT-AET) that induce alignments at the step when the target token is the decoder input, significantly improving alignment accuracy.
papers.conclusion: The proposed methods SHIFT-ATT and SHIFT-AET effectively induce word alignments from Transformer models, with SHIFT-AET achieving state-of-the-art performance without compromising translation quality.
papers.key_findings:
SHIFT-ATT, a pure interpretation method, reduces AER by 7.0-10.2 points over the NAIVE-ATT baseline and 5.5-7.9 points over FAST-ALIGN on three datasets.
SHIFT-AET, which adds and trains an alignment module supervised by SHIFT-ATT alignments, outperforms the statistical aligner GIZA++ by 1.4-4.8 AER points.
A proposed layer selection criterion, based on agreement between source-to-target and target-to-source model alignments, effectively identifies the best layer for alignment induction.
Both SHIFT-ATT and SHIFT-AET improve performance on the downstream task of dictionary-guided decoding compared to the NAIVE-ATT baseline.
Probing experiments show decoder hidden states at lower layers are more relevant to the input token than the output token, validating the shift in alignment step.
future_direction: Extend the study to more downstream tasks and systems.
papers.abstract: Despite its original goal to jointly learn to align and translate, prior researches suggest that Transformer captures poor word alignments through its attention mechanism. In this paper, we show that attention weights DO capture accurate word alignments and propose two novel word alignment induction methods SHIFT-ATT and SHIFT-AET. The main idea is to induce alignments at the step when the to-be-aligned target token is the decoder input rather than the decoder output as in previous work. SHIFT-ATT is an interpretation method that induces alignments from the attention weights of Transformer and does not require parameter update or architecture change. SHIFT-AET extracts alignments from an additional alignment module which is tightly integrated into Transformer and trained in isolation with supervision from symmetrized SHIFT-ATT alignments. Experiments on three publicly available datasets demonstrate that both methods perform better than their corresponding neural baselines and SHIFT-AET significantly outperforms GIZA++ by 1.4-4.8 AER points.

papers.title: Interpreting and improving natural-language processing (in machines) with natural language-processing (in the brain)
papers.research_question: How can brain activity recordings be used to interpret neural network representations, and can aligning models with brain activity improve their language understanding?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a method to interpret neural network representations by aligning them with brain activity recordings, and shows that increasing brain-alignment in BERT improves its performance on syntactic tasks.
papers.conclusion: Aligning NLP models with brain activity can provide insights into their representations and lead to improved language understanding, as demonstrated by improved syntactic performance of brain-altered BERT.
papers.key_findings:
Middle layers of transformers are better at predicting brain activity for longer contexts.
Transformer-XL's performance does not degrade with longer context, unlike other models.
Uniform attention in shallow layers of BERT improves brain activity prediction for contexts up to 25 words.
Altering BERT to have uniform attention in shallow layers improves its performance on syntactic tasks.
Different models (ELMo, USE, BERT, Transformer-XL) encode context information differently.
papers.limitation:
Reverse inference in brain imaging can lead to erroneous conclusions because a brain region can be involved in more than one task.
Direct comparison of performance between different networks is misleading because information is likely organized differently across networks.
papers.abstract: Neural networks models for NLP are typically implemented without the explicit encoding of language rules and yet they are able to break one performance record after another. This has generated a lot of research interest in interpreting the representations learned by these networks. We propose here a novel interpretation approach that relies on the only processing system we have that does understand language: the human brain. We use brain imaging recordings of subjects reading complex natural text to interpret word and sequence embeddings from 4 recent NLP models - ELMo, USE, BERT and Transformer-XL. We study how their representations differ across layer depth, context length, and attention type. Our results reveal differences in the context-related representations across these models. Further, in the transformer models, we find an interaction between layer depth and context length, and between layer depth and attention type. We finally hypothesize that altering BERT to better align with brain recordings would enable it to also better understand language. Probing the altered BERT using syntactic NLP tasks reveals that the model with increased brain-alignment outperforms the original model. Cognitive neuroscientists have already begun using NLP networks to study the brain, and this work closes the loop to allow the interaction between NLP and cognitive neuroscience to be a true cross-pollination.

papers.title: Thinking About Thinking: SAGE-nano's Inverse Reasoning for Self-Aware Language Models
papers.research_question: How can large language models be enabled to introspect on and explain their own reasoning processes, specifically why they choose particular reasoning chains over alternatives?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces inverse reasoning, a paradigm enabling LLMs to introspect on their own reasoning processes via attention pathway reconstruction, and presents SAGE-nano, a 4B-parameter model that demonstrates this capability, improving both reasoning transparency and performance.
papers.conclusion: The inverse reasoning paradigm enables LLMs to introspect on their reasoning and generate interpretable explanations, enhancing transparency and trustworthiness while maintaining competitive performance, establishing foundations for transparent AI systems in safety, education, and scientific discovery.
papers.key_findings:
SAGE-nano achieves competitive reasoning accuracy (e.g., 74.6% on AQUA-RAT) and high explanation quality (92.1% human preference score).
Inverse reasoning enhances both reasoning transparency and forward reasoning performance, as shown by ablation studies.
The model demonstrates superior introspection accuracy in identifying decision points, alternative paths, and confidence calibration.
The architecture can be trained and deployed efficiently on consumer hardware (Mac Mini M1 cluster), making advanced reasoning more accessible.
Inverse reasoning addresses critical AI safety challenges by providing interpretable explanations of model decision-making.
papers.limitation:
The inverse reasoning approach adds significant computational overhead (40% inference time), limiting scalability to larger models.
Current metrics for explanation quality rely heavily on subjective human evaluation; developing automated evaluation metrics remains an open problem.
Inverse reasoning explanations lack objective ground truth, making validation difficult.
The 4-billion parameter constraint limits the model's capacity for complex reasoning tasks compared to larger state-of-the-art models.
future_direction: Investigating inverse reasoning capabilities in larger model architectures (scalability studies).
Extending inverse reasoning to visual and multi-modal reasoning tasks.
Developing robust automated metrics for explanation quality assessment.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities at solving complex reasoning tasks with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting, but their decision-making processes remain somewhat blackbox. We introduce textbfinverse reasoning, a novel paradigm enabling LLMs to decompose and explain their own reasoning chains post-hoc. Our approach, used in SAGE-nano, a 4-billion-parameter reasoning model, employs a metacognitive structure that reflects back via attention processes to identify major decision points and generate explanations of reasoning choices. While typical CoT approaches are directed towards forward reasoning generation, inverse reasoning provides insight into why specific reasoning chains were selected over others. Through thorough testing of logical reasoning puzzles, math problems and ethical dilemmas from AQUA-RAT, CommonsenseQA, and customized benchmarks, we demonstrate that SAGE-nano is at the cutting edge both on reasoning accuracy (74.6% on AQUA-RAT) and explanation quality (92.1% human preference score) for its task, and offers performance almost on par with models like Claude-3.5 Sonnet or GPT-4o. Our contributions are: (i) the first rigorous framework for LLM self-reflection via inverse reasoning, (ii) a novel metalearning framework to reverse the attention flow, (iii) comprehensive evaluation frameworks for reasoning transparency, and (iv) evidence that increasing reasoning using inverse reasoning improves interpretability along with reasoning performance. Our work creates new avenues for transparent AI systems and closes significant gaps in AI safety, education, and scientific discovery.

papers.title: Unveiling Transformers with LEGO: a synthetic reasoning task
papers.research_question: How do Transformer architectures learn to follow a chain of reasoning, and how do architectural choices (like weight tying) and data composition (like pretraining) affect their generalization and the emergence of specific attention patterns?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the LEGO synthetic reasoning task to study how Transformers learn to follow chains of reasoning. It identifies that successful models develop specialized attention heads for association (long-range identity matching) and manipulation (short-range operations), and based on this insight, proposes the LEGO attention module which reduces FLOPs while maintaining or improving performance in large-scale pretraining.
papers.conclusion: The LEGO task provides a controlled setting to understand how Transformers learn reasoning, revealing the importance of structured attention patterns for generalization. These insights can guide architectural design, as demonstrated by the proposed LEGO attention module which offers efficiency gains.
papers.key_findings:
Classical generalization can be deceptive, as models can learn 'shortcut' solutions that do not follow the intended chain of reasoning and impede out-of-distribution generalization.
Iterative architectures like ALBERT, which share weights across layers, exhibit better length extrapolation (generalization to longer reasoning chains) than non-iterative architectures like BERT, suggesting an inductive bias towards implementing a 'for-loop'.
Pretraining helps generalization on the LEGO task primarily by providing a beneficial initialization with structured attention patterns (association and manipulation heads), rather than by encoding complex task-specific knowledge.
Models can be incentivized to learn more robust, iterative solutions through techniques like stochastic depth training, which improves length extrapolation.
The identified structured attention patterns motivate a new LEGO attention module, which when used as a drop-in replacement for standard attention, reduces computational cost and matches or improves performance in large-scale pretraining.
papers.limitation: The study uses a synthetic task, which may not fully capture the complexity of real-world reasoning tasks.
future_direction: Applying the insights from the LEGO task to currently challenging mathematical reasoning tasks like MATH and IsarStep.
Exploring the application of the LEGO attention module to other domains and tasks.
papers.abstract: We propose a synthetic reasoning task, LEGO (Learning Equality and Group Operations), that encapsulates the problem of following a chain of reasoning, and we study how the Transformer architectures learn this task. We pay special attention to data effects such as pretraining (on seemingly unrelated NLP tasks) and dataset composition (e.g., differing chain length at training and test time), as well as architectural variants such as weight-tied layers or adding convolutional components. We study how the trained models eventually succeed at the task, and in particular, we manage to understand some of the attention heads as well as how the information flows in the network. In particular, we have identified a novel \emph{association} pattern that globally attends only to identical tokens. Based on these observations we propose a hypothesis that here pretraining helps for LEGO tasks due to certain structured attention patterns, and we experimentally verify this hypothesis. We also observe that in some data regime the trained transformer finds ``shortcut" solutions to follow the chain of reasoning, which impedes the model's robustness, and moreover we propose ways to prevent it. Motivated by our findings on structured attention patterns, we propose the LEGO attention module, a drop-in replacement for vanilla attention heads. This architectural change significantly reduces Flops and maintains or even \emph{improves} the model's performance at large-scale pretraining.

papers.title: The Power of Question Translation Training in Multilingual Reasoning: Broadened Scope and Deepened Insights
papers.research_question: How broadly can the question alignment framework be applied across diverse reasoning scenarios and model sizes, and what is the mechanism behind its success?
papers.core_contribution: Extends the question alignment framework to diverse reasoning scenarios (chain-of-thought, program-of-thought, common sense) and scales it to extremely large models, providing insights into how it strengthens language alignment and shapes model behavior.
papers.conclusion: The question alignment training framework can be extended to a variety of challenging reasoning scenarios and scales well to extremely large language models, with analysis revealing how it influences the model's internal representation space and reasoning process.
papers.key_findings:
The question alignment framework is broadly applicable, boosting multilingual performance across diverse reasoning scenarios and model families.
Question translation training produces a more unified semantic space, aligning multilingual representations and facilitating the sharing of English expertise.
Proxy-tuning is an efficient alternative to full fine-tuning for extremely large models, achieving near-full-tuning performance without parameter updates.
Incorporating En-X translation data during response alignment can bias the model to generate non-English responses, but at a cost to reasoning accuracy.
Combining question translation and general domain translation data for the alignment stage yields further improvements, especially for low-resource languages.
papers.limitation: There is a trade-off between language consistency (generating responses in the query language) and reasoning accuracy when incorporating En-X translation training, as models perform better with English chain-of-thought.
papers.abstract: Bridging the significant gap between large language model's English and non-English performance presents a great challenge. While some previous studies attempt to mitigate this gap with translated training data, the recently proposed question alignment framework leverages the model's English expertise to improve multilingual performance with minimum usage of expensive, error-prone translation. In this paper, we explore how broadly this method can be applied by examining its effects in reasoning with and without chain-of-thought, as well as with program-of-thought. We also explore applying this framework to extremely large language models in an efficient manner, such as through proxy-tuning. Experiment results on multilingual reasoning benchmarks mGSM, mSVAMP, xCSQA and xNLI demonstrate that we can extend question alignment framework to boost multilingual performance across diverse reasoning scenarios, model families, and sizes. For instance, when applied to the LLaMA2 models, it brings an average accuracy improvements of 12.2% on mGSM even with the 70B model. To understand the mechanism of its success, we analyze representation space, generated response and data scales, and reveal how question translation training strengthens language alignment within LLMs and shapes their working patterns.

papers.title: Language Models Linearly Represent Sentiment
papers.research_question: How is sentiment represented within Large Language Models (LLMs)? Specifically, is sentiment represented linearly and what are the mechanisms involved?
papers.core_contribution: This paper reveals that sentiment is represented linearly in the residual stream of LLMs across multiple models and tasks, and discovers a 'summarization motif' where sentiment is summarized at intermediate tokens like commas and names.
papers.conclusion: The study concludes that sentiment is linearly represented in LLMs and identifies a summarization motif as a key mechanism for sentiment processing, providing a detailed case study for analyzing feature representation in activation space.
papers.key_findings:
Sentiment is represented linearly as a single direction in the residual stream across a range of transformer-based language models.
The sentiment direction found on simple toy datasets generalizes to real-world sentiment analysis tasks like SST and IMDB.
The sentiment direction is causally important for sentiment tasks; intervening on it can flip model predictions.
A 'summarization motif' exists: sentiment information is aggregated at intermediate tokens (e.g., commas, periods, names) without inherent valence, and this summarized information is causally relevant.
Ablating the sentiment direction at comma positions alone significantly reduces classification accuracy, demonstrating the functional importance of the summarization motif.
